{{About|the southern half of planet Earth|use of the term describing astronomical observations|Southern celestial hemisphere}}

[[File:Global hemispheres.svg|thumb|The Southern Hemisphere is highlighted in yellow. The hemispheres appear to be unequal in this image because [[Antarctica]] is not shown.]]
[[File:Southern Hemisphere LamAz.png|thumb|The Southern Hemisphere from above the [[South Pole]]]]

The '''Southern Hemisphere''' is the half ([[Hemispheres of Earth|hemisphere]]) of [[Earth]] that is [[south]] of the [[equator]]. It contains all or part of five [[continent]]s<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.worldatlas.com/aatlas/imageh.htm | title=Hemisphere Map | publisher=WorldAtlas | access-date=13 June 2014 | archive-date=22 April 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422125910/https://www.worldatlas.com/aatlas/imageh.htm | url-status=live }}</ref> (the whole of [[Antarctica]], the whole of [[Oceania]], about 90% of [[South America]], about one-third of [[Africa]], and some islands off the continental [[mainland]] of [[Asia]]) and four [[ocean]]s (the whole [[Southern Ocean]], the majority of the [[Indian Ocean]], the [[Atlantic Ocean|South Atlantic Ocean]], and the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]]), as well as [[New Zealand]] and most of the [[list of islands in the Pacific Ocean|Pacific Islands]] in [[Oceania]]. Its surface is 80.9% water, compared with 60.7% water in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], and it contains 32.7% of Earth's land.<ref>{{cite book|title=Life on Earth: A - G.. 1|date=2002|publisher=[[ABC-CLIO]]|isbn=9781576072868|page=528|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iVEWPg8vnxgC&q=southern+hemisphere+contains+%25+land&pg=PA528|access-date=8 September 2016|archive-date=22 January 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230122160606/https://books.google.com/books?id=iVEWPg8vnxgC&q=southern+hemisphere+contains+%25+land&pg=PA528|url-status=live}}</ref> More than 850 million people live in the Southern Hemisphere, representing around 10–12% of the total global human population.<ref name=":0" />

Owing to the tilt of [[Earth's rotation]] relative to the [[Sun]] and the [[ecliptic|ecliptic plane]], [[summer]] is from December to February (inclusive) and [[winter]] is from June to August (inclusive). September 22 or 23 is the vernal [[equinox]] and March 20 or 21 is the autumnal equinox. The [[South Pole]] is in the centre of the southern hemispherical region.

== Characteristics ==
Southern Hemisphere [[climate]]s tend to be slightly milder than those at similar latitudes in the [[Northern Hemisphere]], except in the [[Antarctic]] which is colder than the [[Arctic]]. This is because the Southern Hemisphere has significantly more ocean and much less land; water heats up and cools down more slowly than land.<ref>Granite specific heat = 0.79 and water = 4.18 J/g⋅K see [[Heat capacity#Table of specific heat capacities]].</ref> The differences are also attributed to oceanic heat transfer and differing extents of greenhouse trapping.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kang |first1=Sarah M. |last2=Seager |first2=Richard |last3=Frierson |first3=Dargan M. W. |last4=Liu |first4=Xiaojuan |title=Croll revisited: Why is the northern hemisphere warmer than the southern hemisphere? |journal=Climate Dynamics |date=March 2015 |volume=44 |issue=5–6 |pages=1457–1472 |doi=10.1007/s00382-014-2147-z |bibcode=2015ClDy...44.1457K }}</ref>

Antarctica's [[Vostok Station]] holds the record for the Southern Hemisphere's lowest temperature at −89.2 °C (−128.6 °F) on July 21, 1983. This is also the lowest temperature ever recorded on earth. The lowest temperature ever recorded in the Northern Hemisphere was a −69.6 °C (−93.3 °F) reading at the Klinck Automatic Weather Station in [[Greenland]] on December 22, 1991.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/wmo-verifies-696degc-greenland-temperature-northern-hemisphere-record|title=WMO verifies -69.6°C Greenland temperature as Northern hemisphere record|date=September 22, 2020|website=World Meteorological Organization}}</ref> The Southern Hemisphere's highest recorded temperature is tied at 50.7 °C (123.3 °F) between [[Oodnadatta]], [[South Australia]], on January 2, 1960, and [[Onslow, Western Australia]], on January 13, 2022.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Is climate change behind record-breaking temperatures in Onslow? - ABC News | url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-01-17/is-climate-change-behind-record-breaking/13708420 | access-date=2026-08-30 | website=www.abc.net.au | date=17 January 2022 }}</ref> Globally, a 1922 reading of 58 °C (136.4 °F) in [[El Azizia]], [[Libya]], was long cited as the world record before the [[World Meteorological Organization]] decertified it in 2012 due to measurement errors. The 56.7 °C (134 °F) temperature recorded in [[Death Valley]], [[California]], on July 10, 1913, replaced the invalidated Libya record.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/markets/commodities/hot-story-libya-loses-temperature-record-to-death-valley-idUSL5E8KD8S3/|title=Hot story: Libya loses temperature record to Death Valley|location=[[Geneva]]|publisher=[[Reuters]]|date=September 13, 2012|access-date=September 9, 2026}}</ref>

[[File:Aurora australis panorama.jpg|left|thumb|upright=1.35|[[Aurora (astronomy)|Aurora australis]] appearing in the night sky of [[Swifts Creek]], {{convert|100|km|abbr=on}} north of [[Lakes Entrance, Victoria]], Australia]]In the Southern Hemisphere, the Sun passes from east to west through the north, although north of the [[Tropic of Capricorn]] the [[Solar time#Mean solar time|mean Sun]] can be directly overhead or due south at midday. The Sun follows a right-to-left trajectory through the northern sky unlike the left-to-right motion of the Sun when seen from the Northern Hemisphere as it passes through the southern sky. Sun-cast shadows turn anticlockwise throughout the day and [[sundial]]s have the hours increasing in the [[Clockwise|anticlockwise]] direction. During [[solar eclipse]]s viewed from a point to the south of the Tropic of Capricorn, the Moon moves from left to right on the disc of the Sun (see, for example, photos with timings of the [[solar eclipse of November 13, 2012]]), while viewed from a point to the north of the [[Tropic of Cancer]] (i.e., in the Northern Hemisphere), the Moon moves from right to left during solar eclipses.

The [[Coriolis effect]] causes cyclones and tropical storms to spin clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, as opposed to [[anticlockwise]] in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/kits/currents/05currents1.html | title=Surface Ocean Currents | publisher=[[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]'s Ocean Service Education  | access-date=13 June 2014 | archive-date=6 July 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170706062957/https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/education/kits/currents/05currents1.html | url-status=dead }}</ref>

The southern [[temperateness|temperate zone]], a subsection of the Southern Hemisphere, is nearly all oceanic.

The [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]] constellation that includes the [[Milky Way|galactic centre]] is a southern constellation as well as both [[Magellanic Clouds]]. This, combined with clearer skies, makes for excellent viewing of the night sky from the Southern Hemisphere with brighter and more numerous stars.[[File:AuroraAustralisDisplay.jpg|left|thumb|Aurora australis appearing from [[Stewart Island|Stewart Island/Rakiura]] in the south of [[New Zealand]]]]

The Southern Hemisphere has significantly less polluted air than the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="poll">{{Cite web|url=https://research.noaa.gov/earth-has-two-different-stratospheres-and-aviation-may-be-to-blame/|title=Earth has two different stratospheres, and aviation may be to blame|first=Theo|last=Stein|date=July 1, 2021}}</ref> This is because most of earth's population and major industrial powers reside in the Northern Hemisphere, including high-emission countries like [[China]] and [[India]].<ref name="poll"/> The Southern Hemisphere was unimpacted by the 1986 [[Chernobyl disaster|Chernobyl nuclear disaster]], which at the time posed a serious threat to the Northern Hemisphere, and which continues to impact certain parts of Europe.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yablokov |first1=Alexey V. |last2=Nesterenko |first2=Vassily B. |title=1. Chernobyl Contamination through Time and Space |journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences |date=November 2009 |volume=1181 |issue=1 |pages=5–30 |doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.2009.04821.x |pmid=20002040 |bibcode=2009NYASA1181....5Y }}</ref> Small traces of radiation from the disaster were found in far off Northern Hemisphere locations like the [[United States]], [[Canada]] and [[Japan]], but there were no traces of radiation at all in the Southern Hemisphere.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_28265/chernobyl-executive-summary|title=Chernobyl: Executive summary|website=Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA)}}</ref>

===Flora and Fauna===
Forests in the Southern Hemisphere have special features which set them apart from those in the Northern Hemisphere. Both [[Chile]] and [[Australia]] share, for example, unique [[beech]] species or ''[[Nothofagus]]'', and [[New Zealand]] has members of the closely related genera ''[[Lophozonia]]'' and ''[[Fuscospora]]''. The [[eucalyptus]] is native to [[Australia]] but is now also planted in [[Southern Africa]] and [[Latin America]] for pulp production, and increasingly, [[biofuel]] uses.

Some African animals like [[chimpanzees]] and [[gorillas]] live in both the Northern and Southern Hemisphere portions of Africa. [[Eastern gorilla]]s are native to three Southern Hemisphere countries; [[Rwanda]] (which is entirely below the equator) and the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and [[Uganda]] (which are trans-hemispheric countries). [[Western gorilla]]s, meanwhile, can be found in [[Angola]], the Democratic Republic of the Congo, [[Equatorial Guinea]], [[Gabon]] and the [[Republic of the Congo]], in addition to being found in the Northern Hemisphere countries [[Cameroon]] and [[Nigeria]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gorillas.org/about-gorillas/gorilla-habitat/|title=The Gorilla Habitat}}</ref> The different species of chimpanzees have a much wider distribution across Africa. The [[common chimpanzee]] occurs in both hemispheres, ranging from the Northern Hemisphere countries of [[Guinea]] and [[Senegal]] in the west to [[Tanzania]] and Uganda in the east. Aside from the population in Tanzania and Uganda, populations in several countries lay partly or wholly south of the equator, including in [[Burundi]], the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Republic of the Congo.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.iucngreatapes.org/chimpanzees |title=Chimpanzees |publisher=IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group Section on Great Apes |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>  The [[bonobo]], which is a distinct species from the common chimpanzee, is exclusive to the Southern Hemisphere. It is endemic to forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo south of the [[Congo River]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://portals.iucn.org/library/sites/library/files/documents/2012-083.pdf |title=Bonobo: Pan paniscus |publisher=IUCN |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> Conversely, the [[western chimpanzee]] subspecies of the common chimpanzee is confined to [[West Africa]] and the Northern Hemisphere. Its present range lies entirely north of the equator, including [[Ghana]], Guinea, [[Guinea-Bissau]], [[Ivory Coast]], [[Liberia]], [[Mali]], Senegal and [[Sierra Leone]].<ref name="IUCN">{{cite iucn |author=Humle, T. |author2=Boesch, C. |author3=Campbell, G. |author4=Junker, J. |author5=Koops, K. |author6=Kuehl, H. |author7=Sop, T. |year=2016 |title=''Pan troglodytes'' ssp. ''verus''  |errata=2016 |volume=2016 |article-number=e.T15935A102327574 |doi=10.2305/IUCN.UK.2016-2.RLTS.T15935A17989872.en |access-date=8 August 2021}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.iucngreatapes.org/western-chimpanzees |title=Western Chimpanzees |publisher=IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group Section on Great Apes |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>

some populations also extend into the Northern Hemisphere, including parts of Kenya (which straddles the equator), [[Ethiopia]] and [[South Sudan]].<ref>{{cite iucn |author=Muller, Z. show a similar pattern: the [[plains zebra]] occurs in certain areas of the [[Horn of Africa]] in the Northern Hemisphere, and southward to Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, [[Malawi]], [[Mozambique]] and much of far southern Africa.<ref>{{cite iucn |author=King, S.R.B. |author2=Moehlman, P.D. |year=2016 |title=''Equus quagga'' |journal=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |volume=2016 African country of [[Lesotho]], but have since gone extinct there, in addition to going extinct in the Southern Hemisphere country Burundi, which is much further north of Lesotho.<ref>{{Cite The [[spectacled bear]] is the only bear species which occurs in the Southern Hemisphere. It is found in certain South American countries like [[Bolivia]], [[Ecuador]] and [[Peru]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iflscience.com/incredible-bears-eye-view-videos-of-andean-bears-reveal-never-before-seen-behaviors-77078|title=Incredible "Bear's-Eye View" Videos Of Andean Bears Reveal Never-Before-Seen Behaviors |work=IFLScience }}</ref> One of the most notable animals to be found almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere is the [[penguin]]. A species is found around [[Isabela Island (Galápagos)|Isabela Island]] on the [[Galápagos Islands|Galápagos]] archipelago in the [[Pacific Ocean]], which straddles the equator.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/world-penguin-new-zealand-earth-antarctica-b1837078.html |first1=Luke |last1=Rix-Standing |title=World Penguin Day: 6 places you'd never have thought you could see them |work=The Independent |date=2021-04-25 |accessdate=2022-03-05 |archive-date=2022-03-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305154318/https://www.independent.co.uk/travel/world-penguin-new-zealand-earth-antarctica-b1837078.html |url-status=live }}</ref> However, most of Isabela and the rest of the archipelago is located in the Southern Hemisphere, and it is deemed by the [[International Hydrographic Organization]] as being wholly within the South Pacific Ocean, rather than the North Pacific.<ref name="IHO1953">{{cite journal |title=Limits of the Oceans and Seas |journal=Nature |date=12 September 1953 |volume=172 |issue=4376 |pages=484 |doi=10.1038/172484b0 |bibcode=1953Natur.172R.484. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Australia and [[Madagascar]] developed many [[Endemism|endemic]] animals due to their geological isolation, including [[kangaroo]]s, [[koala]]s, [[platypus]]es, [[Tasmanian devil]]s, [[emu]]s, [[echidna]]s, [[quokka]]s, [[cassowary|cassowaries]], [[lemur]]s, [[aye-aye]]s, [[fossa (animal)|fossas]], [[indri]]s, [[sifaka]]s and [[panther chameleon]]s. These animals are all native to the Southern Hemisphere, by virtue of being endemic to Australia or Madagascar, with cassowaries and echidnas being found not only in Australia but also in neighboring [[New Guinea]]. [[Dodo]]s were endemic to the formerly uninhabited island of [[Mauritius]], which is located in the [[Indian Ocean]] and Southern Hemisphere. The animal went extinct in 1681, 170 years after the first documented human landing on the island.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nhm.ac.uk/discover/the-dodo-bird-the-real-facts-about-this-icon-of-extinction.html|title=The dodo bird: The real facts about this icon of extinction | Natural History Museum|website=www.nhm.ac.uk}}</ref> Several [[dog breed|domestic dog breeds]] were developed in the Southern Hemisphere, including [[Australian Cattle Dog|Australian cattle dogs]], [[Australian Kelpie|Australian kelpies]], [[Australian Silky Terrier|Australian silky terriers]], [[Australian Terrier|Australian terriers]], [[Bardino Majorero]]s, [[Brazilian Terrier|Brazilian terriers]], [[Bull Arab]]s, [[Chilean Terrier|Chilean terriers]], [[Cimarrón Uruguayo]]s, [[Cordoba Fighting Dog|Cordoba fighting dogs]], [[Dogo Argentino]]s, [[Fila Brasileiro]]s, [[Pampas Deerhound|Pampas deerhounds]], [[Peruvian Hairless Dog|Peruvian Inca orchids]] and [[Tenterfield Terrier|Tenterfield terriers]]. The Dogo Argentino and  Fila Brasileiro are among the most widely banned dog breeds in the world, along with the [[Tosa (dog)|Japanese Tosa Inu]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://highlandcanine.com/blog/dog-breeds-banned-around-the-world/|title=Which Dog Breeds Are Banned Around The World?|first=Jason|last=Purgason|date=October 20, 2023}}</ref> The [[New Guinea singing dog]] naturally occurs on the island of New Guinea, rather than being an intentionally developed breed.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jabcecc.org/ngsd|title=New Guinea Singing Dogs | Animal Conservation|website=JAB Canid Education and Conservation Center}}</ref>

33 kilometers from [[Brazil]]'s Atlantic coast lies [[Ilha da Queimada Grande]], an island commonly known as "Snake Island" due to its large population of venomous [[snake]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/snake-island-brazil-facts|title=The terrifying, deadly island off Brazil that only scientists and soldiers can visit|date=August 9, 2026|website=Discover Wildlife}}</ref> The island is the only known natural habitat of the [[golden lancehead]], a highly venomous species of [[pit viper]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.butantan.gov.br/butantan-educa/como-e-a-ilha-das-cobras-o-que-e-mito-e-o-que-e-realidade-quando-o-assunto-e-o-lar-da-jararaca-ilhoa|title=Como é a Ilha das Cobras: o que é mito e o que é realidade quando o assunto é o lar da jararaca-ilhoa|publisher=Instituto Butantan|date=June 18, 2025}}</ref> Earlier popular estimates claimed hundreds of thousands of snakes, but systematic studies have produced much lower estimates, with several thousand golden lancehead inhabiting the island.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Guimarães|first1=M.|last2=Moreira|first2=F.|last3=Sawaya|first3=R.|title=Population Dynamics of the Critically Endangered Golden Lancehead Pitviper, Bothrops insularis: Stability or Decline?|journal=Journal of Herpetology|year=2014 |volume=9 |issue=4 |article-number=e95203 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0095203 |doi-access=free |pmid=24755842 |pmc=3995933 |bibcode=2014PLoSO...995203G }}</ref> The unusually high concentration is thought to have developed after the island became separated from the mainland, leaving the snake population isolated while providing a relatively predator-poor environment and a seasonal supply of migratory birds; adult golden lanceheads feed primarily on birds, particularly the [[Chilean elaenia]] and [[yellow-legged thrush]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Marques|first=O. A. V.|title=The golden lancehead Bothrops insularis (Serpentes: Viperidae) relies on two seasonally plentiful bird species visiting its island habitat|journal=Journal of Natural History|volume=46|issue=13–14|pages=885–895|year=2012|doi=10.1080/00222933.2011.654278 |bibcode=2012JNatH..46..885M }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/scotttravers/2025/03/27/a-herpetologist-explores-snake-island---home-to-the-worlds-largest-concentration-of-venomous-snakes/|title=A Herpetologist Explores 'Snake Island' — Home To The World's Largest Concentration Of Venomous Snakes|first=Scott|last=Travers |work=Forbes }}</ref>

[[Image:Southern cross appearing on a number of flags.PNG|thumb|upright=1.5|The Southern Cross ([[Crux]]) is a small, distinctive constellation visible predominantly from the skies of the Southern Hemisphere. It is featured on the flags and emblems of several Southern Hemisphere nations, including on the national flags of [[Australia]], [[Brazil]], [[New Zealand]], [[Papua New Guinea]] and [[Samoa]]. It is also featured on other flags such as the flag for the South American trade bloc [[Mercosur]].]]

== Geography ==
There are 48 independent countries fully or partially in the Southern Hemisphere. The number does not take into account countries such as [[France]] and the [[United Kingdom]], which only have land in the Southern Hemisphere via overseas territories and not through their mainlands. 34 of these countries are entirely below the equator. The two northernmost points for countries which have land in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres are [[Colombia]]'s [[Punta Gallinas]] ({{coord|12|27|N|71|39|W|region:CO_type:landmark}}) and [[Somalia]]'s [[Alula Lagoon]] ({{coord|11|59|N|50|47|E|region:UA_type:waterbody|display=inline,title}}). The largest country in the Southern Hemisphere is Brazil and the smallest is [[Nauru]]. 34 of the 48 countries are also situated in the [[Eastern Hemisphere]]; Angola, Australia, Botswana, Burundi, [[Comoros]], the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, [[Eswatini]], Gabon, [[Indonesia]], Kenya, Lesotho, Madagascar, Malawi, [[Maldives]], Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Nauru, [[Papua New Guinea]], Republic of the Congo, Rwanda, [[São Tomé and Príncipe]], [[Seychelles]], [[Solomon Islands]], Somalia, [[South Africa]], Tanzania, [[Timor-Leste]], [[Tuvalu]], Uganda, [[Vanuatu]], Zambia and Zimbabwe. 11 of the 48 countries are also situated in the [[Western Hemisphere]]; [[Argentina]], Bolivia, Brazil, [[Chile]], Colombia, Ecuador, [[Paraguay]], Peru, [[Samoa]], [[Tonga]], and [[Uruguay]]. [[Fiji]], [[Kiribati]] and New Zealand have land in both the Eastern and Western Hemisphere, but are mostly in the Eastern Hemisphere. Kiribati is also one of the 14 countries straddling the equator, making it the only country in the world with land in all four hemispheres (excluding countries with overseas territories).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/which-is-the-only-country-in-the-world-that-spreads-across-all-four-hemispheres.html|title=The Only Country In The World That Spreads Across All Four Hemispheres|first=Benjamin Elisha Sawe in World|last=Facts|date=August 3, 2018|website=WorldAtlas}}</ref> Over half of Kiribati's population live on the capital [[South Tarawa]]. which is in the Eastern Hemisphere and Northern Hemisphere, and the country's default geographical coordinates are {{coord|1|25|N|173|00|E|}}, per the [[centroid]] of the country. Eswatini, Lesotho, New Zealand and Uruguay are the only Southern Hemisphere countries which are entirely outside of the [[tropical climate]] zone, as they are all below the [[Tropic of Capricorn|23°26′S latitude]]. Argentina, Chile and South Africa are mostly outside of the tropical climate zone, although small portions of their land reaches into the tropics.

16 of the 48 countries in the Southern Hemisphere have no [[List of countries and territories by number of land borders|land borders]] to other countries; Australia, Comoros, Fiji, Kiribati, Madagascar, Maldives, Mauritius, Nauru, New Zealand, Samoa, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.<ref name="insular">{{cite journal |last1=Licio |first1=Vania |last2=Pinna |first2=Anna Maria |title=Measuring insularity as a state of nature |journal=Papers in Regional Science |date=August 2021 |volume=100 |issue=4 |pages=979–1005 |doi=10.1111/pirs.12598 |bibcode=2021PRegS.100..979L |hdl=11584/317881 }}</ref> Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Timor-Leste are considered [[divided island]] countries due to having land borders. 11 Southern Hemisphere countries border the [[Atlantic Ocean|South Atlantic Ocean]]; Angola, Argentina, Brazil, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Namibia, Republic of the Congo, São Tomé and Príncipe, South Africa and Uruguay. Colombia's Atlantic coast is technically above the equator, and facing the [[Caribbean Sea]] rather than the open Atlantic. They are the only country with land in the Southern Hemisphere which borders the Caribbean. 13 Southern Hemisphere countries border the Indian Ocean; Australia, Comoros, Indonesia, Kenya, Madagascar, Maldives, Mauritius, Mozambique, Seychelles, Somalia, South Africa, Timor-Leste and Tanzania. Since Colombia's Pacific coast is above the equator, there are 16 rather than 17 Southern Hemisphere countries bordering the South Pacific Ocean; Australia, Chile, Ecuador, Fiji, Indonesia, Kiribati, Nauru, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.<ref name="sailing"/> Bolivia formerly had access to the South Pacific Ocean, but lost it to Chile during the [[War of the Pacific]] in 1879–1884.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://en.unav.edu/web/global-affairs/la-fijaci%C3%B3n-de-bolivia-con-su-perdido-acceso-al-mar|title=Bolivia's 'fixation' with its lost access to the sea. Global Affairs. University of Navarra|website=Global Affairs and Strategic Studies}}</ref>  The landlocked Bolivia still maintains a naval force that trains on [[Lake Titicaca]] and major rivers, as a symbol of hope to one day regain sovereign access to the sea.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.veloso.com/bolivia/sun-island-lake-titicaca/lake-titicaca-insights/the-navy-without-a-coast/|title=The Navy Without a Coast - Sun Island & Lake Titicaca|website=Veloso Tours}}</ref> Despite having no Pacific coast, the country was featured in [[Michael Palin]]'s 1997 series ''[[Full Circle with Michael Palin|Full Circle]]'', where he visited most of the countries on the [[Pacific Rim]].

Aside from Nauru and Kiribati, the countries of the [[Micronesia]] region ([[Federated States of Micronesia]], [[Marshall Islands]] and [[Palau]]) are all entirely above the equator. However, these three North Pacific island nations are sometimes included under the umbrella term "South Pacific", due to their cultural and ecological similarities to the islands of the South Pacific.<ref name="sailing"/> Micronesia's [[Guam]] and [[Northern Mariana Islands]] are overseas territories of the United States, and are similarly associated with the South Pacific despite being located in the North Pacific.<ref name="sailing">''Sailing Directions (planning Guide) for the South Pacific Ocean''. United States: Defense Mapping Agency, Hydrographic/Topographic Center, 1982.</ref> The [[Polynesia]]n U.S. state of [[Hawaii]] is also sometimes associated with the South Pacific label, although it is even further north than the Micronesia region. In 1999, the [[Pacific Islands Forum|South Pacific Forum]] (a regional bloc with Australia, New Zealand and countries in [[Melanesia]], Micronesia and Polynesia) changed its name to the "Pacific Islands Forum", to reflect the fact that most Micronesian islands are in the North Pacific rather than the South Pacific. When the organization first formed in 1971, nearly all modern day Micronesian countries were still colonies of other countries.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia

For geopolitical purposes, many Northern Hemisphere countries are increasingly included in a "[[Global North and Global South|Global South]]" category, to illustrate how countries south of areas like Japan, Europe and North America are less developed, with those regions being referred to as the "Global North" in this context. The "Global South" category sometimes includes countries as far north as [[Mongolia]], while generally excluding Australia and New Zealand on account of them being developed, even though they are two of the southernmost countries on earth.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pressenza.com/2025/10/why-its-time-to-retire-global-north-and-global-south/|title=Why It's Time to Retire 'Global North' and 'Global South'|first=Martina|last=Moneke|work=Pressenza |date=October 7, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://carnegieendowment.org/russia-eurasia/posts/2023/08/the-term-global-south-is-surging-it-should-be-retired|title=The Term 'Global South' Is Surging. ===Oceanography===
====South Pacific====
Most of the South Pacific's islands are divided into the broad ethnographical regions of Melanesia and Polynesia, with the larger island of New Guinea typically being included in Melanesia and New Zealand occasionally in Polynesia. Melanesia includes Fiji, [[New Caledonia]], Solomon Islands and Vanuatu, while Polynesia extends across the central and eastern Pacific and includes areas such as [[American Samoa]], [[Cook Islands]], [[Easter Island]], [[French Polynesia]], [[Niue]], Samoa, [[Tokelau]], Tonga, Tuvalu and [[Wallis and Futuna]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/oceania-human-geography/ |title=Australia and Oceania: Human Geography |publisher=National Geographic Society |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> Australia's east coast and parts of its northern coast are also situated in South Pacific seas, and this is where the [[Great Barrier Reef]] and most of its major cities lay. The volcanic Australian islands of [[Lord Howe Island]] and [[Norfolk Island]] are ecologically similar to tropical South Pacific islands, despite not culturally being considered part of the Melanesia and Polynesia regions.<ref name="tropical">Mueller Dombois, Dieter, and Fosberg, F.R.. ''Vegetation of the Tropical Pacific Islands''. Germany, Springer New York, 1998.</ref> Norfolk Island, while primarily inhabited by [[White people|Caucasian]] Australians, has evidence of prehistoric Polynesian activity from before Europeans discovered the island, as does the United Kingdom's overseas territory the [[Pitcairn Islands]].<ref name="aa">Anderson, Atholl. “Investigating Early Settlement on Lord Howe Island.” Australian Archaeology, no. 57, 2003, pp. 98–102. JSTOR, http://www.jstor.org/stable/40287719. Accessed 11 June 2025.</ref> Additionally, there are certain isolated islands closer to South America, like the [[Desventuradas Islands]], Galápagos Islands and [[Juan Fernández Islands]], which were discovered uninhabited by Europeans and which have no links to Melanesia and Polynesia. However, these are still geologically volcanic/oceanic islands.<ref name="zug">Zug, George R.. ''Reptiles and Amphibians of the Pacific Islands: A Comprehensive Guide''. United States, University of California Press, 2013.</ref><ref name="tropical"/> Some of Indonesia's islands are situated entirely in South Pacific seas, others are situated in the Indian Ocean and some border both ocean systems. Despite this, Indonesia is typically grouped with [[Southeast Asia]] rather than with the rest of the South Pacific.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Pacific-Islands|title=Pacific Islands | Countries, Map, & Facts | Britannica|date=August 8, 2026|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref> Timor-Leste also borders both ocean systems, and is more frequently grouped with the South Pacific than Indonesia is, but is still often regarded as Southeast Asian.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://doi.org/10.1093/irap/lcac005|title=Security cooperation in the Pacific Islands: architecture, complex, community, or something else?|first1=Joanne|last1=Wallis|first2=Henrietta|last2=McNeill|first3=James|last3=Batley|first4=Anna|last4=Powles|date=May 1, 2023|journal=International Relations of the Asia-Pacific|volume=23|issue=2|pages=263–296|via=Silverchair|doi=10.1093/irap/lcac005}}</ref> Since 1945, the [[United Nations]] has categorized Australia, New Zealand, Melanesia, Polynesia and the North Pacific Micronesian islands as part of the continental designation of Oceania, with the term Oceania having been in usage as a descriptor for these areas since the early 19th century. Most sporting organizations like the [[Olympics]] also use this designation, and it is taught as a distinct continent in [[Latin America]] and parts of Europe. For statistical purposes, a [[United Nations|geoscheme]] was created by the United Nations in 1970, which standardized the categorization of countries across the continental designations of Africa, America, Asia, Europe and Oceania.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://unstats.un.org/unsd/methodology/m49/|title=UNSD — Methodology|website=unstats.un.org}}</ref><ref name="Ferrante">{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/geography/the-geoscheme-of-the-united-nations.html|title=The Geoscheme of the United Nations|first=Francesco|last=Ferrante|date=July 13, 2023|website=WorldAtlas}}</ref> The geoscheme definition of Oceania does not include Indonesia or Timor-Leste, which are categorized as part of Asia. This definition also does not include Hawaii or any other North Pacific islands besides the Micronesian ones, in addition to not including the Chilean-administered Easter Island and other South Pacific islands adjacent to South America.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s10551-012-1263-0|title=Business Ethics as Field of Teaching, Training and Research in Oceania|first=Royston|last=Gustavson|date=April 1, 2011|journal=Journal of Business Ethics|volume=104|issue=1|pages=63–72|via=Springer Link|doi=10.1007/s10551-012-1263-0}}</ref>

The Northern Hemisphere Pacific contains a greater concentration of high-latitude and [[subarctic]] islands, including [[Alaska]]'s [[Aleutian Islands]] and several [[Bering Sea]] island groups, as well as [[Russia]]'s [[Kuril Islands]] and [[Sakhalin]].<ref name="world">Tyler, Charles Marion. ''[https://books.google.com.au/books?id=8D5CAAAAIAAJ&pg=PA258&dq=charles+marion+tyler+island+world+of+the+pacific+ocean&hl=en&newbks=1&newbks_redir=1&sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwicw4T5wcSWAxVRkuEIHYHuFZ8Q6AF6BAgJEAM The Island World of the Pacific Ocean]''. United States: S. Carson & Company, 1885.</ref> The Southern Hemisphere has relatively few Pacific islands at comparable latitudes. One of its most notable [[subantarctic]] islands is [[Macquarie Island]], an Australian island at about 54°63′S between [[Tasmania]] and Antarctica.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/antarctic-operations/stations-and-field-locations/macquarie-island/ |title=Macquarie Island research station |publisher=Australian Antarctic Division |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> Macquarie lies north of 60°S and is therefore north of the 60-degree boundary used in the 2002 International Hydrographic Organization definition of the [[Southern Ocean]], although the status of that boundary remains disputed and the 2002 definition has not been universally adopted.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/standards/s-23/S-23_Ed3.0_1953_EN.pdf |title=Limits of Oceans and Seas |publisher=International Hydrographic Organization |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> Along the southern Chilean coast, there are non-oceanic islands at similar latitudes, such as the [[Diego Ramírez Islands]], [[Madre de Dios Island]] and [[Tierra del Fuego]] (which is split with Argentina).<ref name="world"/>

====Southern Indian Ocean====
Along with Madagascar and the west coast of Australia, the southern Indian Ocean also has various smaller volcanic/oceanic landmasses. These include the independent island countries of Comoros, the Maldives, Mauritius and Seychelles, as well as territories such as the [[British Indian Ocean Territory]], Australia's [[Cocos (Keeling) Islands]], [[Christmas Island]] and [[Heard Island and McDonald Islands]], and France's [[Kerguelen Islands]] and [[Réunion]]. The British Indian Territory and  Cocos (Keeling) Islands are oceanic islands which are low-lying [[coral atoll]]s rather than volcanic islands, although they formed on the summits of ancient submarine volcanic structures, while the wider Indian Ocean contains numerous volcanic seamounts and island chains formed by volcanic activity.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://parksaustralia.gov.au/news/investigating-deep-sea-life-indian-ocean-territories/ |title=Investigating deep sea-life in the Indian Ocean Territories |publisher=Parks Australia |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> [[Heard Island]] is especially notable because it contains [[Mawson Peak]], an active volcano that forms part of the [[Big Ben (Heard Island)|Big Ben]] volcanic complex, and the Heard Island and McDonald Islands are described by the Australian Government as home to Australia's only active volcanoes.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://volcano.si.edu/volcano.cfm?vn=234010 |title=Heard |publisher=Smithsonian Institution Global Volcanism Program |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ga.gov.au/scientific-topics/national-location-information/dimensions/remote-offshore-territories/heard-and-mcdonald-islands |title=Heard and McDonald Islands |date=27 June 2014 |publisher=Geoscience Australia |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> The Heard Island and McDonald Islands lie at about 53°S, while the Kerguelen Islands are farther north-west at roughly 49°S. Both are therefore north of 60°S and not part of the Southern Ocean under the IHO's 2002 definition. Even though they are outside the Southern Ocean proper, they are commonly described as subantarctic and are strongly influenced by the Southern Ocean and the [[Antarctic Circumpolar Current]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.antarctica.gov.au/antarctic-operations/stations-and-field-locations/heard-island/location-geography/ |title=Location and geography – Heard Island and McDonald Islands |date=12 August 2026 |publisher=Australian Antarctic Division |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref>

====South Atlantic====
The Atlantic Ocean has several extremely isolated islands in the Southern Hemisphere. By comparison, the North Atlantic has few isolated islands outside of [[Bermuda]] and the [[Azores]], which themselves are less remote than the South Atlantic islands. Aside from the non-oceanic [[Falkland Islands]], the South Atlantic includes islands like [[Ascension Island]], [[Saint Helena]], [[South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands]], and [[Tristan da Cunha]]. Many of these are [[British Overseas Territories]]: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha form one British territory, while the Falklands and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands are separate British Overseas Territories.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.gov.uk/types-of-british-nationality/british-overseas-territories-citizen |title=Types of British nationality: British overseas territories citizen |publisher=GOV.UK |access-date=3 September 2026}}</ref> Tristan da Cunha is generally regarded as the most remote inhabited island on earth.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/a-thousand-miles-from-nowhere-83203/|title=A Thousand Miles from Nowhere - NASA Science|date=February 26, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nationalgeographic.org/explore/programs/pristine-seas/expedition-tristan-da-cunha|title=Tristan da Cunha|website=National Geographic Society}}</ref>  Brazil's uninhabited [[Trindade and Martim Vaz]] lie 1,100 kilometers from the Brazilian mainland, and are among the most remote South Atlantic islands administered by a non-European nation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Trindade e Martim Vaz |url=https://www.gov.br/icmbio/pt-br/assuntos/biodiversidade/unidade-de-conservacao/unidades-de-biomas/marinho/lista-de-ucs/mona-das-ilhas-de-trindade-e-martim-vaz-e-do-monte-columbia |publisher=Instituto Chico Mendes de Conservação da Biodiversidade |access-date=29 August 2026}}</ref> At the far southern edge of the Atlantic lies the [[Norway|Norwegian]] dependency of [[Bouvet Island]], a volcanic island largely covered by [[glaciers]]. It is highly isolated from any other landmasses, and close to the boundary of the Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean and Southern Ocean. Bouvet Island is often labelled as the most remote island on earth, and was used as a setting in the 2004 film ''[[Alien vs. Predator (film)|Alien vs. Predator]]'', due to its extreme geography.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-46547254|title=Climate secrets of the world's most remote island|date=December 14, 2018|website=www.bbc.com}}</ref> The United Nations geoscheme officially categorizes the island as part of South America, although it is closer to Antarctica and Africa.<ref name="Ferrante" />

===Geology===
Among Southern Hemisphere countries, Australia, Fiji, Indonesia, Maldives, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, and Vanuatu are fully or partially on the [[Indo-Australian Plate]], with Fiji, New Zealand, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu also lying across boundaries with the [[Pacific Plate]] and smaller plates.<ref name="Bird2003">{{cite journal |last1=Bird |first1=Peter |year=2003 |title=An updated digital model of plate boundaries |journal=Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=1027 |article-number=2001GC000252 |doi=10.1029/2001GC000252 |bibcode=2003GGG.....4.1027B }}</ref> Indonesia and Papua New Guinea occupy one of the most geologically complex regions on earth, being situated on the boundaries of the Indo-Australian Plate, Pacific Plate, [[Banda Sea Plate]], [[Bird's Head Plate]], [[Caroline Plate]], [[Eurasian Plate]], [[Maoke Plate]], [[Philippine Sea Plate]], [[Sunda Plate]] and [[Woodlark Plate]], among other smaller plates and microplates.<ref>https://www.gns.cri.nz/our-science/land-and-marine-geoscience/ Geoscience resources.</ref><ref name="Bird2003"/> The Indo-Australian Plate also includes the British Indian Ocean Territory, New Caledonia and Australia's Christmas Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Lord Howe Island and Norfolk Island.<ref name="Bird2003"/> Heard Island and McDonald Islands and the Kerguelen Islands lie on the [[Antarctic Plate]] as the main exposed peaks of the mostly submerged [[Kerguelen Plateau]]. The Antarctic Plate also includes Bouvet Island.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Quilty | first1=PG | last2=Wheller | first2=GE | title=Heard Island and the McDonald Islands: A window into the Kerguelen Plateau | journal=Papers and Proceedings of the Royal Society of Tasmania | date=2000 | pages=1–12 | doi=10.26749/rstpp.133.2.1 | url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/266348005 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Kerguelen Plateau |url=https://www.ga.gov.au/scientific-topics/energy/province-sedimentary-basin-geology/petroleum/offshore-southern-australia/kerguelen-plateau |website=Geoscience Australia}}</ref> The Pacific Plate extends deep into the Northern Hemisphere, and includes parts of the mainland Americas such as [[Los Angeles]], [[San Diego]] and [[Mexico]]'s [[Baja California Peninsula]], but it is principally associated with smaller islands in the Southern Hemisphere, including American Samoa, Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Niue, Pitcairn Islands, Samoa, Tokelau, Tuvalu and Wallis and Futuna.<ref>https://geology.com/articles/san-andreas-fault.shtml</ref><ref>https://pubs.usgs.gov/bul/2195/b2195.pdf {{Bare URL PDF|date=October 2026}}</ref> Macquarie Island lies on the boundary of the Indo-Australian Plate and Pacific Plate, while Tonga lies on the boundary of the Pacific Plate and [[Tonga Plate]].<ref name="Bird2003"/> The [[South American Plate]] does not include various South Pacific islands politically associated with South America, but does include Ascension Island, the Falklands Islands and Trindade and Martim Vaz. The [[Nazca Plate]] is a major plate off the Pacific coast of South America and includes Chile's Desventuradas Islands, Easter Island, Juan Fernández Islands and [[Salas y Gómez Island]], as well as Ecuador's Galápagos Islands. The largest landmass on the Nazca Plate is Isabela Island in the Galápagos Islands. The Nazca Plate is adjacent to active regional structures including the [[Easter Microplate]] and [[Galápagos Microplate]].<ref name="Bird2003"/> The [[Scotia Plate]] is associated with the [[South Sandwich Islands]], while [[South Georgia]] lies within the complex Scotia–South American tectonic boundary region.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Seismotectonics and relative plate motions in the Scotia Sea region |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/JB094iB06p07293 |journal=Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth |date=1989}}</ref> Several countries and islands associated with Africa lie fully or partially on the [[Somali Plate]], including Comoros, Kenya, Madagascar, Mauritius, [[Mayotte]], Mozambique, Réunion, Seychelles, Somalia and Tanzania.<ref name="Bird2003"/> The [[African Plate]] encompasses a large portion of the South Atlantic, including Saint Helena and Tristan da Cunha, which are thousands of kilometers from mainland Africa.<ref>https://www.geoworldtravel.com/resources/Mid_Atlantic/Geology%20TristanStHelAscen.pdf {{Bare URL PDF|date=October 2026}}</ref>

== Demographics, economy and human geography ==
===Population===
[[File:Apollo17WorldReversed.jpg|thumb|right|A photo of Earth from [[Apollo 17]] (''[[The Blue Marble|Blue Marble]]'') with the South Pole at the top and the continent of Africa]]

More than 850 million people live in the Southern Hemisphere, representing around 10–12% of the total global human population.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/90-of-people-live-in-the-northern-hemisphere-2012-5|title=90% Of People Live In The Northern Hemisphere - Business Insider|date=4 May 2012|work=Business Insider|access-date=3 January 2023|archive-date=19 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180119181108/http://www.businessinsider.com/90-of-people-live-in-the-northern-hemisphere-2012-5|url-status=live}}</ref> Of those 850 million people, more than 203 million live in Brazil. Approximately 93% of Brazil is below the equator, and over 95% of the total population also live below the equator.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Brazil's population reaches 213.4 million — MercoPress | url=https://en.mercopress.com/2025/08/29/brazil-s-population-reaches-213.4-million | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250829170707/https://en.mercopress.com/2025/08/29/brazil-s-population-reaches-213.4-million | access-date=2026-08-28 | archive-date=2025-08-29}}</ref> More than 150 million live in Indonesia's [[Java]], the most populous island in the world and one which is situated entirely below the equator. The most populous country in the Southern Hemisphere is Indonesia, with 275 million people.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldatlas.com/articles/countries-located-completely-in-the-southern-hemisphere.html|title=Countries Located Completely in the Southern Hemisphere|first=Ferdinand Bada in World|last=Facts|date=August 29, 2019|website=WorldAtlas}}</ref> Roughly 30 million Indonesians live north of the equator on the northern portions of the islands of [[Sumatra]], [[Borneo]], and [[Sulawesi]], as well as most of [[North Maluku]]. The rest of the population lives in the Southern Hemisphere, making Indonesia the country with the most inhabitants in the Southern Hemisphere.{{citation needed|date=October 2020}} The most populous country entirely located within the Southern Hemisphere is Tanzania, with an estimated population of roughly 67 million people as of 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/tanzania|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109103650/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/tanzania|url-status=dead|archive-date=January 9, 2021|title=CIA – The World Factbook – Tanzania|publisher=Cia.gov|access-date=11 May 2025}}</ref> In terms of size, Colombia is the ninth largest overall country with any land in the Southern Hemisphere, and has a population of 53 million, although much of Colombia is above the equator. The portion of Colombia below the equator is the same size as European countries like [[Croatia]] and the [[Netherlands]], and makes up the [[Amazonas Department, Colombia|Amazonas Department]]. Colombia's most populated settlement in the Southern Hemisphere is the Amazonas Department capital city [[Leticia, Amazonas|Leticia]], with other Southern Hemisphere settlements being [[El Encanto]], [[La Chorrera, Colombia|La Chorrera]], [[La Pedrera, Amazonas|La Pedrera]], [[Mirití-Paraná]], [[Puerto Alegría]], [[Puerto Arica]], [[Puerto Nariño]], [[Puerto Santander, Amazonas|Puerto Santander]] and [[Tarapacá, Amazonas|Tarapacá]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldometers.info/world-population/colombia-population/|title=Colombia Population (2026)|website=Worldometer}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Leticia (Municipality, Colombia) | url=https://citypopulation.de/en/colombia/admin/amazonas/91001__leticia/ }}</ref><ref name="estimates">{{citation|author=DANE |author-link=National Administrative Department of Statistics |title=Resultados y proyecciones (2005-2020) del censo 2005 |url=http://www.dane.gov.co/files/investigaciones/poblacion/proyepobla06_20/ProyeccionMunicipios2005_2020.xls |access-date=2018-07-15 |work=Censo 2005 |place=Colombia |language=es}}.</ref> Somalia has a population of 20 million, and the vast majority of the country is above the equator. Somalia's biggest settlement in the Southern Hemisphere is [[Kismayo]], which had a population of 458,000 in 2014.<ref>[https://populationstat.com/somalia/kismaayo PopulationStat] Population of Kismayo, city and urban area</ref> The Northern and Southern Hemisphere portions of Kenya are similar in size to each other, but the country's population is concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere, with the three most populated cities [[Nairobi]], [[Mombasa]] and [[Nakuru]] being below the equator.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldometers.info/population/largest-cities-in-kenya/|title=Largest Cities by Population in Kenya|website=Worldometer}}</ref>

In 2026, the states with the highest [[population density]] in the Southern Hemisphere were Mauritius and Nauru, which respectively had 618 people and 595 people per square [[kilometer]].<ref name="pop"/> Maldives had a higher population density than Mauritius and Nauru, with 1,945 people per kilometer, however, most of its population lives above the equator, with only a small portion of the country being in the Southern Hemisphere. In 2026, the least densely populated states in the Southern Hemisphere were Namibia and Australia, which had 4 people and 3 people per square kilometer.<ref name="pop">{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/List-of-Countries-Dependencies-and-Territories-by-Population-Density|title=List of Countries, Dependencies, and Territories by Population Density | Statistics, Rank, & Most Crowded | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260823234947/https://www.britannica.com/topic/List-of-Countries-Dependencies-and-Territories-by-Population-Density |archive-date=23 August 2026 }}</ref> In 2026, Australia also ranked as the second least densely populated state in the Eastern Hemisphere, behind only Mongolia.<ref name="pop"/> Over 87% of Australia's population live within just 50 kilometers of coastal areas.<ref name="auscoastalpop">{{cite web |url=https://soe.dcceew.gov.au/coasts/pressures/population |title=Population |publisher=Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, Australian Government |access-date=2026-09-11}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Population {{!}} Australia state of the environment 2021 | url=https://soe.dcceew.gov.au/coasts/pressures/population | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220719235318/https://soe.dcceew.gov.au/coasts/pressures/population | access-date=2026-08-28 | archive-date=2022-07-19}}</ref> Australia's Indian Ocean west coast is much more sparsely populated than its Pacific east coast, with [[Perth]] being the only major city on the west coast. Like Australia's Indian Ocean coast, Namibia's Atlantic coast is also very sparsely populated.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.australiangeographic.com.au/news/2010/06/skeleton-coast-namibias-strange-desert-dwellers/|title=Skeleton Coast: Namibia's strange desert dwellers|first=A. G.|last=Staff|date=June 1, 2010}}</ref> Four countries or territories in the Southern Hemisphere currently have no permanent human population; Bouvet Island, [[French Southern and Antarctic Lands]] (which includes the Kerguelen Islands), Heard Island and McDonald Islands and South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. These territories have their own [[Country code top-level domain|internet country codes and domain names]], despite the lack of human activity.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://archive.osb.org/geog/countrycodes.html|title=Internet Country Codes, Digraphs, Used in Internet Domain Names ( ISO 3166 )|website=archive.osb.org}}</ref>

Among the largest metropolitan areas in the Southern Hemisphere are [[Jakarta]] (33 million people), [[São Paulo]] (22 million), [[Kinshasa-Brazzaville]] (19 million), [[Buenos Aires]] (16 million), [[Rio de Janeiro]] (12 million), [[Lima]] (11 million), [[Surabaya metropolitan area|Surabaya]] (10 million), [[Luanda]], [[Bandung metropolitan area|Bandung]] (9 million each), [[Dar es Salaam]], [[Santiago]] (7 million each), [[Johannesburg]], [[Semarang metropolitan area|Semarang]], [[Belo Horizonte]] (6 million each), [[Sydney]], [[Melbourne]] and [[Cape Town]] (5 million each). Melbourne is the southernmost city in the world with a population exceeding one million.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Özsungur |first1=Fahri |title=Nexus of AI, Climatology, and Urbanism for Smart Cities |date=2024 |publisher=IGI Global Scientific Publishing |page=130 |isbn=979-8-3693-5920-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hO86EQAAQBAJ&dq=%22melbourne%22+%22southernmost%22+city+%22million%22&pg=PA130 |access-date=8 May 2026}}</ref>

===Language===
[[Portuguese language|Portuguese]] is one of the most spoken languages in the Southern Hemisphere, with over 230 million speakers in six countries – mostly in Brazil, but also in Angola, Mozambique, Timor-Leste, and small parts of São Tomé and Príncipe that lie south of the equator.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uc.pt/international-applicants/oportunidades/linguas/economic_potential_portuguese.pdf|title=Potencial Económico da Língua Portuguesa|website=University of Coimbra|access-date=2017-05-15|archive-date=2021-10-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211024163947/https://www.uc.pt/international-applicants/oportunidades/linguas/economic_potential_portuguese.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Spanish language|Spanish]] is the primary language in Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Equatorial Guinea, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay. [[French language|French]] is an official language in Gabon, French Polynesia, Mayotte, New Caledonia, Réunion and Wallis and Futuna, but is not necessarily the most widely spoken language in all of these locations.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.newcaledonia.travel/pro/promoting-the-archipelago/thematic-fact-sheets/local-expressions/|title=Languages and Local Expressions in New Caledonia | New Caledonia Tourism|website=New Caledonia Tourism: The official website for tourism in New Caledonia}}</ref> [[English language|English]] is a primary language in Ascension Island, Australia, the British Indian Ocean Territory, the Falkland Islands, New Zealand, Norfolk Island, Saint Helena, Tristan da Cunha, Tuvalu and Uganda. English and [[Tuvaluan language|Tuvaluan]] (a [[Polynesian language]]) are the official joint languages of Tuvalu, while [[Luganda]] is the most widely spoken language in Uganda, despite the official administrative language being English.<ref>{{Cite web | title=#KYR: Tuvalu - Information {{!}} The Cove | url=https://cove.army.gov.au/article/kyr-tuvalu-information | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251126025056/https://cove.army.gov.au/article/kyr-tuvalu-information | access-date=2026-09-08 | archive-date=2025-11-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://theconversation.com/english-rules-in-uganda-but-local-languages-shouldnt-be-sidelined-49381|title=English rules in Uganda, but local languages shouldn't be sidelined|first1=Judith|last1=Nakayiza|first2=Medadi|last2=Ssentanda|editor-first1=Natasha |editor-last1=Joseph |date=November 5, 2015|website=The Conversation|doi=10.64628/AAJ.hjeywdppc}}</ref> Most of the other countries and states in the Southern Hemisphere have primary languages which are their own local languages rather than colonial languages. English is widely understood in South Africa, but the country has 12 official languages recognized by its national constitution, with [[Zulu language|Zulu]] being the most widely spoken.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://southafrica-info.com/arts-culture/the-languages-of-south-africa/|title=The languages of South Africa|first=Mary|last=Alexander|date=June 8, 2026}}</ref> Some authors use the term "Southern Hemisphere English" to describe similarities between the English spoken in areas such as Australia, the Falkland Islands, New Zealand and South Africa.<ref>Gramley, Stephan., Gramley, Vivian., Pätzold, Kurt-Michael. ''A Survey of Modern English''. United Kingdom: Taylor & Francis, 2020.</ref> Outside of English and languages from immigrant communities, Australia also has more than 250 Indigenous languages, including 800 dialects. Each language is specific to a particular place and people.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aiatsis.gov.au/explore/languages-alive|title=Languages alive|first=Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander|last=Studies|date=October 13, 2025|website=aiatsis.gov.au}}</ref> Australia itself has no official language, even though English is the most widely spoken.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sbs.com.au/voices/article/no-asian-language-signs-please-were-australian/xnjoyti3k|title=No Asian language signs please, we're Australian|date=May 16, 2018|website=SBS Voices}}</ref>

On the Pitcairn Islands in the South Pacific, English is spoken alongside a Polynesian-influenced dialect called [[Pitkern]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thelanguagecloset.com/2023/04/29/pitkern-norfuk/|title=The English spoken in Earth's most geographically isolated island|date=April 29, 2023}}</ref> Native Polynesian or [[Melanesian languages]] are most common on the majority of South Pacific islands, with the colonial language of English also typically being understood.<ref name="ling"/> Kiribati and Nauru are the only countries or territories in the South Pacific which speak languages related to the [[Micronesian language|Micronesian language family]]. All others are located entirely in the North Pacific, although Kiribati itself has various islands in the North Pacific, since the country straddles the equator.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Nauruan classification | url=https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/download/4717/4360/8035 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251207200021/https://journals.linguisticsociety.org/proceedings/index.php/PLSA/article/download/4717/4360/8035 | archive-date=2025-12-07}}</ref><ref>Petersen, Glenn. ''Traditional Micronesian Societies: Adaptation, Integration, and Political Organization in the Central Pacific''. Hong Kong, University of Hawaii Press, 2009.</ref> The only oceanic South Pacific islands which speak Spanish are Ecuador's Galápagos Islands and Chile's Juan Fernández Islands and Easter Island.<ref name="ling"/> Residents of Easter Island also still speak [[Rapa Nui language|a native Polynesian language]] which developed before the island became part of Chile in 1888.<ref name="ling">{{cite book |editor-last=Bowen |editor-first=J. Donald |title=Linguistics in Oceania, 2 |publisher=De Gruyter Mouton |date=1971 |doi=10.1515/9783111418810 |isbn=978-3-11-141881-0 }}</ref> Spanish is not spoken on Chile's oceanic Desventuradas Islands and Salas y Gómez Island, as these islands are uninhabited by civilians. The island of New Guinea is estimated to have around 7,000 living languages. New Guinea, which is split between Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, makes up roughly 10% of the world's languages, despite having less than 0.1% of the world's population.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/papua-new-guinea-has-more-living-languages-than-any-other-country|title=Papua New Guinea has more living languages than any other country|website=Our World in Data}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lowyinstitute.org/the-interpreter/papua-new-guinea-learning-lessons-language|title=Papua New Guinea: Learning the lessons of language|date=August 17, 2026|website=The Lowy Institute}}</ref>

Comoros is the only [[Arabic language|Arabic]]-speaking country entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ablcc.org/resources/arab-country-profiles/comoros|title=Comoros|first=|last=|website=www.ablcc.org}}</ref> Somalis speak both Arabic and [[Somali language|Somali]]. The two countries are members of the [[Arab League]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.arabamerica.com/why-is-the-comoros-in-the-arab-league/|title=Why is The Comoros in the Arab League?|first=Evan|last=Ploeckelman|date=August 17, 2021}}</ref> Comoros is also the only Arabic-speaking country which is a borderless island country; [[Bahrain]] is naturally an island but is connected to [[Saudi Arabia]] through man-made infrastructure, whilst the people of [[Malta]] speak their own distinct language which is related to Arabic.<ref>https://www.um.edu.mt/library/oar/bitstream/123456789/28326/1/THE%20MALTESE%20AND%20THE%20ARABIC%20DIALECTS.pdf {{Bare URL PDF|date=October 2026}}</ref>

===Business and media===

[[Elon Musk]] was born in the Southern Hemisphere in [[Pretoria]], South Africa, and currently has the highest personal net worth in the world. It reincorporated itself from an Australian company to an American company in 2004, and was delisted from the Australian stock exchange that same year.<ref>{{cite web
 |title=News Corporation Limited corporate restructure 2004: Background
 |url=https://www.ato.gov.au/forms-and-instructions/news-corporation-limited-corporate-restructure-2004/background
 |website=Australian Taxation Office

 |access-date=9 July 2026

The film's director [[James Cameron]] has lived in New Zealand since 2012, and has said that the indigenous Polynesian cultures of areas like New Zealand partially inspired the alien world of the film.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://people.com/all-about-real-events-that-inspired-avatar-11870592|title=What Inspired the 'Avatar' Franchise? Inside the Real-Life Events, Cultures and Religious Deities That Informed the Story}}</ref> The highest-grossing film shot entirely in the Southern Hemisphere is the 2003 [[New Line Cinema]] film ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King]]'', which grossed $1,147,997,407 and was shot in New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.the-numbers.com/|title=The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King (2003) - Box Office and Financial Information|website=The Numbers}}</ref>

Television began relatively early in several of the more economically developed Southern Hemisphere countries. Brazil became the second country in Latin America to have regular television broadcasts when [[TV Tupi]] began broadcasting in São Paulo on September 18, 1950.<ref>{{cite web|title=TV brasileira completa 75 anos e se prepara para nova revolução com a chegada da TV 3.0|url=https://www.gov.br/anatel/pt-br/assuntos/noticias/tv-brasileira-completa-75-anos-e-se-prepara-para-nova-revolucao-com-a-chegada-da-tv-3.0|website=Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações|date=18 September 2025|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>{{efn|name=MexicoTV|The first television station in Mexico began regular broadcasts on September 1, 1950, after months of sporadic tests. See the [[XHTV]] article.}} Argentina followed in 1951, when [[Canal 7 (Argentina)|Canal 7]] began regular broadcasting in Buenos Aires on October 17, making it one of the earliest television countries in the Americas.<ref>{{cite web|title=17 de octubre de 1951: inicia sus transmisiones Canal 7, el primer canal de televisión argentina|url=https://cultura.legislatura.gob.ar/cultura_posts/17-de-octubre-de-1951-inicia-sus-transmisiones-canal-7-el-primer-canal-de-television-argentina961.html|website=Legislatura de la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires|date=17 October 2023|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> Australia introduced television in September 1956, with [[TCN]] in Sydney making the country's first regular television transmission on September 16, followed by other stations including [[HSV-7]] in Melbourne and the [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation|ABC]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Introducing television to Australia, 1956|url=https://www.naa.gov.au/help-your-research/fact-sheets/introducing-television-australia-1956|website=National Archives of Australia|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Welcome to television, 1956|url=https://www.nfsa.gov.au/stories/articles/welcome-television-1956|website=National Film and Sound Archive of Australia|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> Chile also developed television during the 1950s: the [[Pontifical Catholic University of Valparaíso]] conducted the country's first wireless television transmission on October 5, 1957, while university television services were established publicly during the following years.<ref>{{cite web|title=Historia|url=https://ucvtv.cl/quienes-somos/|website=UCV TV|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Los orígenes de la televisión chilena|url=https://www.memoriachilena.gob.cl/602/w3-article-761.html|website=Memoria Chilena|publisher=Biblioteca Nacional de Chile|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> New Zealand began regular television broadcasting on June 1, 1960, initially from [[Auckland]].<ref>{{cite web|title=New Zealand's first official TV broadcast|url=https://nzhistory.govt.nz/first-official-tv-broadcast|website=Manatū Taonga — Ministry for Culture and Heritage|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> Indonesia began its national television era with [[TVRI]] on August 24, 1962, initially broadcasting coverage of the [[1962 Asian Games]].<ref name="auto">{{cite web|title=Sejarah|url=https://ppid.tvri.go.id/page/sejarah|website=Televisi Republik Indonesia|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>

The spread of television was generally slower in poorer or more remote Southern Hemisphere areas. However, South Africa, despite being the most industrialized country in Africa at the time, did not begin nationwide television broadcasting until January 1976. This is because the government had delayed the introduction of the medium for years; experimental broadcasts only began in 1975.<ref>{{cite web|title=The First Ever SABC TV Broadcast in SA|url=https://web.sabc.co.za/sabc/home/tvob/events/details?id=c01a1640-7f2b-4270-82c3-caea284ad8ad&title=The+First+Ever+SABC+TV+Broadcast+in+SA|website=South African Broadcasting Corporation|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> The comparatively late adoption of television in South Africa contrasted with the earlier arrival of television in a number of poorer African territories. In smaller Pacific islands, the high cost of transmitters, imported equipment and national distribution networks, combined with small populations and geographic isolation, heavily delayed the development of television services. Fiji, for example, began experimental television broadcasting in 1991 and regular service in 1994.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The JoW7ll1l <if Pacffo; Studies, Volume 32 no. 2, 2012|url=https://fjdigitallib.usp.ac.fj/greenstone3/jps/sites/jpssite/collect/jps/index/assoc/HASH01d4/f601e1ef.dir/doc.pdf|journal=Journal of Pacific Studies|publisher=University of the South Pacific|date=2012|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> In the Galápagos Islands, television broadcasting began in 1980 with Tele Galápagos in [[Puerto Baquerizo Moreno]], around two decades after commercial television had begun on mainland Ecuador; it initially had only a low-power transmitter and limited local coverage.<ref>{{cite web|title=Historia humana Santa Cruz|url=https://www.galapagos.gob.ec/wp-content/uploads/downloads/2021/02/Historia-humana-Santa-Cruz.pdf|website=Gobierno del Ecuador|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref><ref>Matelski, Marilyn J.. ''Soap Operas Worldwide: Cultural and Serial Realities''. United Kingdom, McFarland, Incorporated, Publishers, 1999.</ref> On Easter Island, [[Televisión Nacional de Chile]] established a television station at [[Hanga Roa]] on January 24, 1975. Initially, programmes were prerecorded on the Chilean mainland and transported to the island, while live satellite transmission from Santiago began in 1996; additional terrestrial networks were introduced later.<ref>{{cite web|title=Memoria anual 2022|url=https://estaticos.tvn.cl/skins/web-assets/images/corporativo/2022/memoria-anual-2022.pdf|website=Televisión Nacional de Chile|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>

Like in the Northern Hemisphere, television broadcasting subsequently became a major cultural industry throughout the Southern Hemisphere. Australia developed several large national networks, including the ABC, [[Special Broadcasting Service|SBS]], [[Seven Network]], [[Nine Network]] and [[Network 10]], while New Zealand's principal television broadcaster has been [[TVNZ]]. Brazil became home to [[TV Globo|Globo]], one of the world's largest television networks, while Argentina developed major broadcasters including [[Telefe]] and [[El Trece]]. Chile developed networks including [[Chilevisión]], [[Canal 13 (Chile)|Canal 13]] and [[Mega (Chilean TV network)|Mega]], while South Africa developed the [[South African Broadcasting Corporation]] (SABC) alongside commercial broadcasters such as [[e.tv]]. Indonesia's major television market developed around broadcasters including TVRI, [[RCTI]], [[SCTV (TV network)|SCTV]] and [[Indosiar]].<ref name="auto"/> In the Southern Hemisphere, some networks have also had international corporate ownership. Until 2025, U.S. media conglomerate [[Paramount Global]] controlled Network 10 in Australia, Telefe in Argentina and Chilevisión in Chile, meaning that major free-to-air networks in three geographically distant Southern Hemisphere markets were for a period under common ownership.<ref>{{cite web|title=Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2023|url=https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/813828/000081382824000007/para-20231231.htm|website=U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission|access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>

===Currency===
The currencies of the Southern Hemisphere reflect a mixture of national monetary systems, regional currency unions, and countries that use another state's currency. Australia's [[Australian dollar]] (AUD) is also used as legal tender in Kiribati, Nauru and Tuvalu.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.westernunion.com/blog/en/us/australian-currency/|title=Money in Australia guide | Exchanging Australian dollars (AUD)|website=Blog | Western Union}}</ref> [[New Zealand dollar|New Zealand's dollar]] (NZD) is used by New Zealand and also by its Polynesian territories the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau, while the Pitcairn Islands also use it despite being a British territory.<ref>{{cite web |title=Cook Islands banking |url=https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/-/media/project/sites/rbnz/files/regulation-and-supervision/berl-cook-island-banking-special-report-december-2022 |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> The [[United States dollar]] (USD) is the official currency of Ecuador, including its Galápagos Islands, and is also the official currency of Timor-Leste, where the [[Banco Central de Timor-Leste|Central Bank of Timor-Leste]] issues centavo coins equivalent in value to US cents.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ecuador adopts the US dollar as legal tender |url=https://www.bce.fin.ec/seguridades-en-billetes-y-monedas/ |publisher=Central Bank of Ecuador |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Know your Money |url=https://www.bancocentral.tl/en/go/know-your-money |publisher=Banco Central de Timor-Leste |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> In Africa, [[Central African CFA franc]] (XAF) is shared by Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo, while Comoros uses the separate [[Comorian franc]]; in southern Africa, [[South African rand|South Africa's rand]] forms the basis of the [[Common Monetary Area]], linking South Africa, Eswatini, Lesotho and Namibia, with Eswatini's [[Swazi lilangeni|lilangeni]] and Lesotho's [[Lesotho loti|loti]] pegged to the rand and Namibia's [[Namibian dollar]] maintained at parity with it.<ref>{{cite web |title=Currency |url=https://www.centralbank.org.sz/currency/ |publisher=Central Bank of Eswatini |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> Most of the remaining Southern Hemisphere states issue national currencies, including the [[Argentine peso]], [[Bolivian boliviano]], [[Brazilian real]], [[Chilean peso]], [[Colombian peso]], [[Paraguayan guaraní]], [[Peruvian sol]] and [[Uruguayan peso]] in South America; the [[Angolan kwanza]], [[Botswana pula]], [[Burundian franc]], [[Congolese franc]], [[Kenyan shilling]], [[Malagasy ariary]], [[Malawian kwacha]], [[Mauritian rupee]], [[Mozambican metical]], [[Rwandan franc]], [[São Tomé and Príncipe dobra]], [[Seychellois rupee]], [[Somali shilling]], [[Tanzanian shilling]], [[Ugandan shilling]], [[Zambian kwacha]] and [[Zimbabwe Gold]] in Africa; and the [[Indonesian rupiah]], [[Maldivian rufiyaa]], [[Fijian dollar]], [[Papua New Guinean kina]], [[Samoan tālā]], [[Solomon Islands dollar]], [[Tongan paʻanga]] and [[Vanuatu vatu]] in Asia and Oceania. Some non-independent Southern Hemisphere territories add several further currency systems: French Polynesia, New Caledonia and Wallis and Futuna all use the [[CFP franc]] (XPF), the common currency of France's Pacific collectivities, issued by the [[Institut d'émission d'outre-mer]];<ref>{{cite web |title=IEOM: central bank of the French Pacific collectivities |url=https://www.ieom.fr/ |publisher=Institut d'émission d'outre-mer |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref> American Samoa uses the US dollar, while French territories such as Réunion and [[Mayotte]] use the [[euro]]. Christmas Island, the Cocos (Keeling) Islands and Norfolk Island use the Australian dollar as they are Australian external territories. Easter Island uses the Chilean peso because it is part of Chile, rather than having a separate island currency.<ref>{{cite web |title=Frequently Asked Questions about Easter Island |url=https://www.easterisland.travel/easter-island-facts-and-info/faq/ |access-date=2 September 2026}}</ref>

===Tourism===
Popular tourist destinations in the Southern Hemisphere include [[Bali]], [[Buenos Aires]], Cape Town, Easter Island, Lima, Rio de Janeiro, Sydney and [[Tahiti]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Bahamondes |first=Bianca |url=https://www.thedailymeal.com/travel/10-best-southern-hemisphere-destinations-where-it-will-soon-be-summer-slideshow/slide-6 |title=10 Best Southern Hemisphere Destinations Where It Will Soon Be Summer |publisher=The Daily Meal |date=2016-11-17 |access-date=2022-03-05 |archive-date=2022-03-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305223553/https://www.thedailymeal.com/travel/10-best-southern-hemisphere-destinations-where-it-will-soon-be-summer-slideshow/slide-6 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.travelnation.co.uk/tours/tailor-made-holidays/southern-hemisphere-round-the-world-holiday-with-easter-island-and-tahiti|title=Southern Hemisphere round the world holiday with Easter Island and Tahiti|website=Travel Nation|access-date=2022-03-05|archive-date=2022-03-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220305230556/https://www.travelnation.co.uk/tours/tailor-made-holidays/southern-hemisphere-round-the-world-holiday-with-easter-island-and-tahiti|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2016, Lima was the most visited city in the Southern Hemisphere, and the 32nd most visited city in the world. The other Southern Hemisphere cities in the top 100 that year were Sydney, Johannesburg, Melbourne, São Paulo, Buenos Aires, Jakarta, Rio de Janeiro, Cape Town, [[Montevideo]], [[Durban]] and [[Quito]]. According to a 2017 report, the most popular Southern Hemisphere "[[kick the bucket|bucket list]]" destinations among Australians were Antarctica, New Zealand, the Galápagos Islands, South Africa and Peru.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/from-antarctica-to-botswana-aussies-set-for-summer-exodus/news-story/aff91c1407a581250f7009f470d871af|url-access=subscription|title=Aussies set for summer exodus|newspaper=The Australian}}</ref> Quito, Ecuador is the closest major city to the [[equator|equatorial line]] on the planet, and [[Ushuaia, Argentina]] claims the title of world's southernmost city. Ushuaia's default geographical coordinates are {{coord|54|48|S|68|18|W|}}. Cape Town, [[Christchurch]], [[Hobart]], [[Punta Arenas]] and Ushuaia are officially acknowledged as the five international [[Antarctic gateway cities]] that serve as primary entry points for travel to the Antarctic region.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Antarctic Cities: From Gateways to Custodial Cities |journal=[[Western Sydney University]] |url=https://researchdirect.westernsydney.edu.au/islandora/object/uws:60135 |last1=Salazar |first1=Juan Francisco |pages=193 |last2=James |first2=Paul |year=2021 |department=Institute for Culture and Society |publication-place=[[Penrith, New South Wales]] |isbn=9781741085280 |last3=Leane |first3=Elizabeth |last4=Magee |first4=Liam}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |url=https://antarcticaffairs.org/a-door-to-the-ice-the-significance-of-the-antarctic-gateway-cities-today/ | first = Gabriela | last = Roldan | year = 2015 | pages = 58–70 | title = A door to the ice?: the significance of the Antarctic Gateway Cities today | volume = 2 | journal = Journal of Antarctic Affairs }}</ref>
