===Standard of living===
Among the most developed nations in the Southern Hemisphere is Australia, with a nominal GDP per capita of US$63,487 and a [[Human Development Index]] (HDI) of 0.946, the tenth-highest in the world as of the 2024 report. New Zealand is also well developed, with a nominal [[GDP]] per capita of US$48,072 and an HDI of 0.939, putting it at number 16 in the world in 2024. The least developed nations in the Southern Hemisphere cluster in Africa and Oceania, with Mozambique and Burundi at the lowest ends of the HDI, at 0.461 (number 183 in the world) and 0.420 (number 187 in the world), respectively. The nominal GDPs per capita of these two countries do not go above US$650, a tiny fraction of the incomes enjoyed by Australians and New Zealanders. In 2025, the French overseas territory French Polynesia had the highest life expectancy for both males and females in the Southern Hemisphere (81.9 years for males and 86.6 years for females).<ref name="life">{{Cite web|url=https://www.worlddata.info/life-expectancy.php|title=Average life expectancy by country|website=Worlddata.info}}</ref> French Polynesia also had the highest life expectancy for males and females in the Western Hemisphere, above countries such as the United States and Canada. In 2025, Africa's Lesotho had the lowest life expectancy for both males and females in the Southern Hemisphere (55.0 years for males and 60.4 years for females).<ref name="life"/> The only countries with lower life expectancies for males and females in 2025 were the Northern Hemisphere African countries of the [[Central African Republic]], [[Chad]] and Nigeria.<ref name="life"/>

Nauru, which was under Australian administration between 1914 and 1968, had one of the highest GDP per capitas in the world during the 1970s and 1980s, due to its [[phosphate]] industry. It eventually suffered an economic collapse, following a decline in its phosphate and misguided financial decisions. Before the economic collapse, Nauru was earning 70 times more than its island neighbors were.<ref name="bank">{{Cite web | url=https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/952141468141870800/pdf/ESM3210Experiences1Oil1Fund01PUBLIC1.pdf | title=Experiences with Oil Funds: Institutional and Financial Aspects | website=[[Worldbank]] | date=June 2006}}</ref> During this time, Nauru's government spent money on a [[West End of London|London West End]] musical and lost over a billion dollars on lavish property development projects in Australia, Hawaii and the [[Philippines]].<ref name="bank"/><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hawaikitower.org/about-us-1|title=Hawaiki Tower About Us|website=hawaikitower}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gfparchitects.com/project/pacific-star-building/|title=Pacific Star Building - GFP Architects|website=gfparchitects.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Crocombe|first1=Ron|title=Asia in the Pacific Islands : replacing the West|date=2007|publisher=IPS Publications, University of the South Pacific|location=Suva, Fiji|isbn=978-9820203884|page=169|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iDg9oAkwsXAC&dq=%22Manila+Pacific+Star+Hotel%22&pg=PA169}}</ref> The [[Nauru House]] in Melbourne was briefly the city's tallest building, and had to be sold by the government of Nauru to pay off debts.<ref>{{cite news|last1=McAloon |first1=Cath |url=http://www.theage.com.au/articles/2004/04/17/1082140116981.html |title=Receivers take over Nauru House|work=[[The Age]]|date=18 April 2004|access-date=22 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040511162536/http://www.theage.com.au/articles/2004/04/17/1082140116981.html|archive-date=11 May 2004|url-status=dead}}</ref> Nauru currently receives income from Australia by hosting detained [[asylum seeker]]s, and had the second lowest GDP in the world in 2025, behind only Tuvalu, which is also in the Southern Hemisphere. Tuvalu is increasingly affected by rising sea levels, which have encouraged some residents to consider migration out of the country. Under the 2023 [[Falepili Union]], Australia established a pathway for Tuvaluan citizens to live, work, and study in Australia. In its first year, around two-thirds of Tuvalu's population applied for the visa, although places were initially limited.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.dfat.gov.au/geo/tuvalu/australia-tuvalu-falepili-union-treaty |title=Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union treaty |website=[[Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Australia)|Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade]] |access-date=1 September 2026}}</ref>

===Sporting culture===
[[Association football]] is generally the most popular sport across the Southern Hemisphere, particularly in South America, Indonesia and much of Southern Africa. It is the dominant spectator and participation sport in nearly all South American countries, while football has also become the most widely followed sport across much of Africa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/868932/soccer-interest-worldwide-countries/?srsltid=AfmBOop6jW8E7iKaIIuT4Qn7Vvk_6zBY9Liiu3sLbFmY3fbJ7HRbGWE4|title=Country with most soccer fans worldwide 2026|website=Statista}}</ref> South America is strongly associated with football, having produced numerous internationally successful national teams and clubs, although some South American countries retain additional sporting traditions that differ from the continental norm.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.worldfootball.net/country-ranking/ |title=World Football Elo Ratings |publisher=World Football Elo Ratings |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> [[Cricket]] is particularly prominent in Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, all of which have longstanding domestic competitions and internationally successful national teams; it is also followed extensively in other parts of the Southern Hemisphere, including Namibia and Zimbabwe.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.icc-cricket.com/about/members/associates |title=ICC Members |publisher=International Cricket Council |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> [[Rugby union]] has a similarly strong Southern Hemisphere presence, especially in Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the islands of Melanesia and Polynesia. In the South Pacific, rugby union is the national sport of Fiji, New Zealand, Samoa and Tonga, and is among the region's most prominent sports.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.world.rugby/organisation/membership/oceania |title=Oceania Rugby |publisher=World Rugby |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> In South America, rugby union has a particularly strong following in Argentina and Uruguay, which have traditions considerably stronger than those found in most other South American countries; both are members of [[Sudamérica Rugby]], the continental governing body for the sport.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.world.rugby/organisation/membership/south-america |title=Sudamérica Rugby |publisher=World Rugby |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref>

[[Rugby league]], which is a distinct sport from Rugby union, has a more geographically limited following. It is one of Australia's major football codes and has a strong presence in [[New South Wales]] and [[Queensland]], while Papua New Guinea is notable for being the only country where rugby league is regarded as the national sport and enjoys exceptionally widespread popular support.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nrl.com/about/annual-report/ |title=National Rugby League annual reports |publisher=National Rugby League |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pngolympiccommittee.org/sports/rugby-league/ |title=Rugby League |publisher=Papua New Guinea Olympic Committee |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> Papua New Guinea is set to gain a club in Australia's top Rugby league competition the [[National Rugby League|NRL]] in 2028.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nrl.com/news/2024/12/12/papua-new-guinea-to-join-the-nrl-in-2028/|title=Papua New Guinea to join the NRL in 2028|date=December 12, 2024|website=National Rugby League}}</ref> The NRL has additionally had a team from New Zealand competing since 1995, with Rugby league being significantly less popular in New Zealand than Rugby union. Australia is also the birthplace of [[Australian rules football]], a code whose popularity is concentrated in [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]], [[South Australia]], [[Western Australia]], Tasmania and the [[Northern Territory]], including major urban centers such as [[Adelaide]], Melbourne and Perth. It is comparatively less dominant in Sydney and [[Brisbane]], where rugby league and other football codes have historically had stronger followings; this geographical division is associated with a concept known as the [[Barassi Line]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.afl.com.au/about-afl/what-is-afl |title=Australian Football |publisher=Australian Football League |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.afl.com.au/news/1459318/aussie-rules-participation-hits-record-625000-participants-in-2025 |title=Aussie Rules participation hits record 625,000 participants in 2025 |publisher=Australian Football League |date=2026 |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> Outside Australia, Nauru is particularly notable for the prominence of Australian rules football. The sport was introduced there during the period of Australian administration and became established as the island's national sport, making Nauru the only country outside Australia where Australian rules football is the most popular sport.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nauru.gov.nr/media/190841/nauru_bulletin__11_3nov2022__245_.pdf |title=Nauru Bulletin |publisher=Government of Nauru |date=2022 |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> Association football remains comparatively undeveloped in Nauru, and the country is one of the few sovereign states not affiliated with [[FIFA]]. FIFA currently has 211 member associations, and Nauru is absent from its membership list, along with some other Micronesian countries which lie above the equator, including the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://inside.fifa.com/en/about-fifa/associations |title=Member Associations |publisher=FIFA |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://naurusoccer.com/about-us/ |title=About Us |date=28 May 2024 |publisher=Nauru Soccer Federation |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> In 1995, Nauru invested one million dollars in the nearly bankrupt [[Fitzroy Football Club|Fitzroy Lions]], which competed in the [[Australian Football League|AFL]], Australia's top national league for Australian rules football.<ref name="zer">{{Cite web|url=https://www.zerohanger.com/what-if-an-island-covered-in-bird-poo-had-saved-fitzroy-afl-143920/|title=What if an island covered in bird poo had saved Fitzroy?|first=Zero|last=Hanger|date=2 October 2023}}</ref> However, shortly afterwards there was a change in leadership in Nauru, and the new governors concluded that any projects in operation were to be halted, with audits into every single one of the island's offshore ventures to be conducted. Nauru's new governors were granted legal advice that it would be improper to continue propping up an insolvent business such as the Fitzroy Lions, and the club eventually had to merge with the [[Brisbane Bears]], becoming the [[Brisbane Lions]] in 1997, after having been in the competition as Fitzroy since 1897.<ref name="zer"/>

Australia's national association football team the [[Australia men's national soccer team|Socceroos]] used to compete in [[FIFA]]'s [[Oceania Football Confederation]], but switched to the [[Asian Football Confederation]] in 2006. This was partially due to a lack of competition from the smaller Pacific island teams in the OFC. In a 2001 OFC qualifying match for the [[FIFA World Cup]], the Socceroos had a [[Australia 31–0 American Samoa|31–0 win over American Samoa]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/only-eleven-for-the-aussies-this-time-1.380789|title=Only eleven for the Aussies this time|newspaper=[[The Irish Times]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.socceroos.com.au/news/watch-australia-31-0-american-samoa-20-years-ago-today |title=Watch: Australia 31-0 American Samoa, 20 years on |publisher=Socceroos |date= 11 April 2021|accessdate=2022-01-19}}</ref> The American Samoa game became the largest international victory in the history of the sport, breaking the record set in Australia's previous qualifying match, where they [[Tonga 0–22 Australia|defeated Tonga 22–0]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.independent.ie/sport/soccer/american-samoa-finally-get-17-year-monkey-off-their-back-26795800.html|title=American Samoa finally get 17-year monkey off their back|website=Irish Independent|date=26 November 2011 }}</ref> In the American Samoa game, [[Archie Thompson]] also broke the record for most goals in an international match, scoring 13.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://socceroos.com.au/news/archies-135-year-revelation-another-player-scored-13-goals-one-game|title=Archie's 135-year revelation: Another player scored 13 goals in one game! | Socceroos|date=April 11, 2020|website=socceroos.com.au}}</ref> The subsequent trials and tribulations in American Samoan football were documented in the 2023 [[Searchlight Pictures]] film ''[[Next Goal Wins (2023 film)|Next Goal Wins]]''. The film was directed by New Zealander [[Taika Waititi]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-01-02/next-goal-wins-review-taika-waititi-american-samoan-soccer/103270868|title=Taika Waititi was once a renegade. Does his new movie measure up?|work=ABC News |date=January 1, 2024|via=www.abc.net.au}}</ref>

Unlike Nauru and other Micronesian countries, Kiribati is currently an associate member of the Oceania Football Confederation. However, Kiribati is not a member of FIFA itself, and consequently cannot participate in FIFA competitions such as the FIFA World Cup. Tuvalu has the same status: both are currently the OFC's associate members and neither has FIFA membership.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.oceaniafootball.com/32nd-ofc-ordinary-congress-commences-in-vancouver-canada/ |title=32nd OFC Ordinary Congress commences in Vancouver, Canada |publisher=Oceania Football Confederation |date=1 May 2026 |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.oceaniafootball.com/a-new-chapter-for-football-in-kiribati-begins-with-ofc-visit/ |title=A new chapter for football in Kiribati begins with OFC Visit |publisher=Oceania Football Confederation |date=3 September 2026 |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> The Galápagos Islands have historically had no football association affiliated with the [[Ecuadorian Football Federation]] and consequently have not had a representative club in Ecuador's principal national league system. FIFA has nevertheless documented an organised local football scene on the islands, with neighbourhood leagues in [[Santa Cruz Island (Galápagos)|Santa Cruz]], [[San Cristóbal Island|San Cristóbal]] and [[Isabela Island (Galápagos)|Isabela]]. Among the islands, there is a provincial championship whose winner travels 1,000 kilometers to mainland Ecuador to represent Galápagos in the amateur national neighbourhood-league competition.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://inside.fifa.com/es/news/islas-galapagos-un-paraiso-para-el-futbol-barrial |title=Islas Galápagos: un paraíso para el fútbol barrial |publisher=FIFA |date=12 June 2020 |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref> Remote Chilean islands in the South Pacific have also developed unorthodox ways to represent themselves in football. Easter Island has long maintained its own national football team despite being part of Chile, while the Juan Fernández Islands have also developed a representative side. The Juan Fernández Islands are members of [[Non-FIFA international football|Conselho Sul-Americano de Novas Federações de Futebol]], which is for teams that are not recognised by South America's [[CONMEBOL]] federation. They have played multiple matches against Easter Island, who are unconfirmed members of [[CONIFA]], a similar organization for national teams not recognized by FIFA. The Easter Island team's first match in 1996 was a 5–3 away win against the Juan Fernández Islands at [[Robinson Crusoe Island]]; Easter Island have also played against the national team of the Falkland Islands, who likewise aren't recognized by FIFA.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beaumont |first1=Adam |last2=Düerkop |first2=Sascha |title=Small States and Territories Against a Giant: The Organisation History of Football in Oceania |journal=The International Journal of the History of Sport |volume=42 |issue=12–13 |pages=1510–1532 |date=2025 |doi=10.1080/09523367.2025.2579850}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://inside.fifa.com/news/easter-island-amateur-football-at-its-purest |title=Easter Island: Amateur Football at Its Purest |publisher=FIFA |access-date=4 September 2026}}</ref>

===Religion and human history===
Before the [[Age of Discovery]], most of the Southern Hemisphere was largely cut off from the cultural constructs of the [[Western world|Western]] and [[Eastern world]]s.<ref name="hempower">{{cite web |url=https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/167446/SI61Sthn_hemisphere_power.pdf |accessdate=17 March 2022 |title=Australia as a Southern Hemisphere power |author=Benjamin Reilly |publisher=Australian Strategic Policy Institute |website=www.files.ethz.ch |date=July 2013 |archive-date=28 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328132207/https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/167446/SI61Sthn_hemisphere_power.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Some view the geopolitical concepts of the West and the East as being Northern Hemisphere-centric concepts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Paton |first1=Michelle |last2=Chengmin |first2=Zhang |title=Southern culture and the North/South divide: More than a metaphor |journal=Journal of the Oriental Society of Australia |date=January 2014 |volume=46 |pages=26–40 |url=https://search.informit.org/doi/abs/10.3316/INFORMIT.340931605527016 }}</ref> The most geographically widespread religion in the modern Southern Hemisphere is the colonial religion of [[Christianity]], prevalent in South America, Africa, Oceania, and Timor-Leste. [[Islam]] is common in certain areas of East Africa as well as in Indonesia, [[Hinduism]] is mostly concentrated on/around the islands of [[Bali]], Mauritius and Fiji.<ref>{{cite web |author=Analysis |url=https://assets.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2014/01/global-religion-full.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180323215026/http://assets.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2014/01/global-religion-full.pdf |archive-date=2018-03-23 |url-status=live |title=Global religious landscape|publisher=Pewforum.org |date=19 December 2011 |access-date=17 August 2012}}</ref> In the Southern Hemisphere, [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Orthodox Christianity]] is less common than [[Catholicism]] and other forms of Christianity such as [[Protestantism]]. It is concentrated among small [[Eastern Europe]]an and [[Balkans|Balkan]] immigrant communities in countries like Australia and Brazil.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2017/11/08/orthodox-christianitys-geographic-center-remains-in-central-and-eastern-europe/|title=1. Orthodox Christianity's geographic center remains in Central and Eastern Europe|date=November 8, 2017}}</ref> Large proportions of the population in Australia and New Zealand are increasingly not affiliated to any religion, with the majority of New Zealand's population currently classified as unaffiliated.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.stats.govt.nz/news/losing-our-religion/|title=Losing our religion | Stats NZ|website=www.stats.govt.nz}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.publicservice.govt.nz/data/workforce-data/demographics/religion|title=Religion|website=Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho}}</ref> This mirrors trends in other developed [[Asia-Pacific]] countries above the equator, such as China, Japan and South Korea, which also have large proportions of the population not affiliated to any religion.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thediplomat.com/2026/02/why-did-buddhism-decline-in-asia/|title=Why Did Buddhism Decline in Asia?}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.christianitytoday.com/2024/06/pew-east-asia-christians-buddhists-korea-hong-kong-taiwan/|title=East Asians Leave Childhood Religion Most in World, but Remain Spiritual|first=Isabel|last=Ong|date=June 17, 2024}}</ref> Religious unaffiliation is less common in Australia and New Zealand's Christian-majority South Pacific island neighbors.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/feature/religious-composition-by-country-2010-2020/|title=Religious Composition by Country, 2010-2020|date=June 9, 2025|website=Pew Research Center}}</ref> Most of the world's [[Jews|Jew]]ish population is concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere countries of [[Israel]] and the United States. Southern Hemisphere countries which rank in the top 15 for global Jewish populations are Argentina (170,000), Australia (117,000), Brazil (90,030) and South Africa (49,500).<ref name="vir">{{Cite web|url=https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jewish-population-of-the-world|title=Vital Statistics: Jewish Population of the World|website=Jewish Virtual Library}}</ref> Argentina, Australia, Brazil and South Africa collectively only make up 2.5% of the global Jewish population.<ref name="vir"/> The experiences of Jews in Southern Hemisphere countries like Argentina, Australia and South Africa are often collectively grouped together, since these locations are geographically isolated from the places where most of the global Jewish population reside.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/1396077|title=Jewish Frontier Experiences in the Southern Hemisphere: The Cases of Argentina, Australia, and South Africa|author=Elazar, Daniel J.|year=1983|journal=Modern Judaism|volume=3|issue=2|pages=129–146|doi=10.1093/mj/3.2.129 |jstor=1396077 |via=JSTOR}}</ref> Additionally, various [[Jewish holiday]]s are deeply connected to specific seasons of the Northern Hemisphere, which do not correlate with the seasons of the Southern Hemisphere.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chabad.org/parshah/article_cdo/aid/3582740/jewish/Why-Are-Jewish-Holidays-Pegged-to-the-Agricultural-Cycle.htm|title=Why Are Jewish Holidays Pegged to the Agricultural Cycle?|first=Lazer|last=Gurkow|website=www.chabad.org}}</ref>

The oldest continuously inhabited city in the Southern Hemisphere is [[Bogor]], in western [[Java]], which was founded in 669. Ancient texts from the Hindu kingdoms prevalent in the area definitively record 669 CE as the year when Bogor was founded. However, some evidence shows that [[Zanzibar City|Zanzibar]], an ancient port with around 200,000 inhabitants off the coast of Tanzania, may be older than Bogor. A Greco-Roman text written between 1 and 100 CE, the [[Periplus of the Erythrean Sea|''Periplus of the Erythraean Sea'']], mentioned the island of ''Menuthias'' ([[Ancient Greek]]: Μενουθιάς) as a trading port on the east African coast, which is probably the small Tanzanian island of [[Unguja]] on which Zanzibar is located. The oldest monumental civilizations in the Southern Hemisphere are the [[Norte Chico civilization]] and [[Casma–Sechin culture]] from the northern coast of Peru. These civilizations built cities, pyramids, and plazas in the coastal river valleys of northern Peru with some ruins dating back to 3600 BCE. Easter Island, located about {{Convert|3,500|km|abbr=on}} from Chile and French Polynesia, is considered to be the most remote place on Earth to have been permanently inhabited by humans before the Age of Discovery.<ref>Hemm, Robert & Mendez, Marcelo. (2003). ''Aerial Surveys of Isle De Pasqua: Easter Island and the New Birdmen''. 10.1007/978-1-4615-0183-1_12</ref> It was settled by a Polynesian group known as the [[Rapa Nui people|Rapa Nui]].

Areas of the Southern Hemisphere that had no known contact with humans before the Age of Discovery include the British Indian Ocean Territory, Christmas Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Heard Island and McDonald islands, the Kerguelen Islands, Mauritius and Seychelles (in the Indian Ocean), the Desventuradas Islands, the Galápagos Islands, [[Jarvis Island]], the Juan Fernández Islands, Lord Howe Island and Macquarie Island (in the South Pacific), [[Annobón]], Ascension Island, Bouvet Island, [[Fernando de Noronha]], Saint Helena, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, Trindade and Martim Vaz and Tristan da Cunha (in the South Atlantic) and Antarctica. Some of these locations eventually received human populations following European discovery, including Annobón, Ascension Island, the British Indian Ocean Territory, Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Christmas Island, Fernando de Noronha, the Galápagos Islands, the Juan Fernández Islands, Lord Howe Island, Mauritius, Saint Helena, Seychelles and Tristan da Cunha, while the other locations remain uninhabited by civilians. Mauritius and Seychelles became their own independent countries in 1968 and 1976, and are some of the only nation states in the world without true Indigenous populations.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://aii.unimelb.edu.au/mauritius-one-step-closer-to-diego-garcia-sovereignty/|title=Mauritius One Step Closer to Diego Garcia Sovereignty - Australia India Institute|first=Maisha|last=Samiha|date=October 14, 2024}}</ref> The Falkland Islands were found uninhabited by British mariner [[John Strong (mariner)|John Strong]] in 1690, although a 2021 study claimed indigenous South Americans may have visited the islands between 1275 and 1420, without ever having a long-term occupation. This study has not been acknowledged by the government of the Falkland Islands.<ref name="phys">{{Cite web|url=https://phys.org/news/2021-10-team-evidence-prehistoric-human-falkland.html|title=Team discovers evidence of prehistoric human activity in Falkland Islands|date=October 27, 2021}}</ref><ref name="falklands1592"/>  Norfolk Island, the Pitcairn Islands and New Zealand's [[Auckland Islands]] were discovered uninhabited yet are generally accepted to have had Polynesian activity beforehand, as there is archeological evidence to support this.<ref>{{cite web | title=The First Real Settlement: A Polynesian 'mystery island' | Discover Norfolk Island | date=25 November 2021 | url=https://www.norfolkisland.net/the-first-real-settlement-a-polynesian-mystery-island/ }}</ref><ref name=auckland1806>{{cite web |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/parks-and-recreation/places-to-go/southland/places/subantarctic-islands/auckland-islands/ |title=Auckland Islands |publisher=New Zealand Department of Conservation |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=Pre-Mutineer History | url=https://library.puc.edu/pitcairn/pitcairn/history-pre-mutineer.shtml | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040720170441/http://library.puc.edu:80/pitcairn/pitcairn/history-pre-mutineer.shtml | access-date=2026-09-08 | archive-date=2004-07-20}}</ref>

==== Timeline of European exploration in the Southern Hemisphere ====
* '''1470:''' {{flagicon|São Tomé and Príncipe}} [[São Tomé]] — Portuguese navigators, traditionally identified as [[João de Santarém]] and [[Pêro Escobar]], reached São Tomé on December 21, which was Saint Thomas's Day. December 21, 1470 is the date cited by the government of São Tomé and Príncipe, although a date of December 21, 1471 has also been cited.<ref name="saotome1470">{{cite web |url=https://turismo.gov.st/en/pourquoi-sao-tome-et-principe/culture-et-patrimoine/journey-through-ages |title=A Journey Through the Ages |publisher=Government of São Tomé and Príncipe |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref><ref name="saotome1470b">{{cite web |url=https://eve.fcsh.unl.pt/en/places/sao-tome-island |title=São Tomé island |publisher=Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion, Universidade Nova de Lisboa |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref> Only a small part of the island of São Tomé is in the Southern Hemisphere, and the following year, the Portuguese reached the neighboring island [[Príncipe]], which is entirely above the equator.<ref name="saotome1470"/>
* '''1473:''' {{flagicon|Equatorial Guinea}} [[Equatorial Guinea]] —  Portuguese sailors reached the previously uninhabited island of Annobón on January 1, during the exploration of the [[Gulf of Guinea]]. Its name derives from the Portuguese ''Ano Bom'' ("good year"). The exact attribution of the navigator is disputed, although modern scholarly work commonly associates the discovery with [[Fernão do Pó]].<ref name="annobon1473">{{cite book |title=Biodiversity Conservation in the Gulf of Guinea Oceanic Islands: Recent Progress, Ongoing Challenges, and Future Directions |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-06153-0_24 |publisher=Springer Nature |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-06153-0_24 |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref><ref name="annobon1473b">{{cite web |url=https://eve.fcsh.unl.pt/en/node/5151 |title=Ano Bom island |publisher=Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion, Universidade Nova de Lisboa |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref> Annobón is the only part of Equatorial Guinea which is in the Southern Hemisphere, and the Portuguese had already reached Northern Hemisphere areas of Equatorial Guinea during the previous year.<ref name="bioko1472">{{cite web |url=https://eve.fcsh.unl.pt/en/places/fernando-po-island |title=Fernando Pó Island |publisher=Encyclopaedia of Portuguese Expansion, Universidade Nova de Lisboa |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref><ref name="bioko1472b">{{cite web |url=https://www.dge.mec.pt/noticias/educacao-para-cidadania/premio-de-investigacao-fernando-po |title=Prémio de Investigação Fernando Pó |publisher=Direção-Geral da Educação, Portugal |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref>
* '''1482:''' {{flagicon|Democratic Republic of the Congo}} [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and {{flagicon|Republic of the Congo}} [[Republic of the Congo]] — [[Diogo Cão]] reached the mouth of the Congo River in 1482, making this the earliest documented European contact with territory of the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo and Republic of the Congo.<ref name="congo1482">{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Diogo-Cao|title=Diogo Cão | Explorer, Navigator, Africa | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref>
* '''1482:''' {{flagicon|Angola}} [[Angola]] — After reaching the Congo River in 1482, Diogo Cão subsequently sailed south along the coast of present-day Angola.<ref name="angola1482">{{cite web |url=https://www.angola50anos.gov.ao/pt/Historial-de-Angola |title=Historial de Angola |publisher=Government of Angola |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1487–1488:''' {{flagicon|Namibia}} [[Namibia]] — [[Bartolomeu Dias]] sailed along the southern African coast and landed in the vicinity of present-day [[Walvis Bay]] during his voyage of 1487–1488.<ref name="namibia1487">{{cite web |url=https://sahistory.org.za/dated-event/portuguese-navigator-bartholomew-dias-erects-first-stone-cross-south-african-coast |title=Portuguese navigator Bartholomew Dias erects the first stone cross on the South African coast |publisher=South African History Online |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1488:''' {{flagicon|South Africa}} [[South Africa]] — Bartolomeu Dias reached the southern African coast in 1488 and became the first European known to set foot on present-day South African territory, landing at [[Mossel Bay]].<ref name="namibia1487"/>
* '''1498:''' {{flagicon|Mozambique}} [[Mozambique]] — Portuguese mariner [[Vasco da Gama]] reached the coast of Mozambique during his first voyage to India in 1498.<ref name="mozambique1498">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mozambique.co.za/About_Mozambique-travel/mozambique-info.html|title=Northern Mozambique - History, Ivory & Slaves, Vasco da Gama|website=www.mozambique.co.za}}</ref>
* '''1498:''' {{flagicon|Kenya}} [[Kenya]] — Vasco da Gama reached the East African coast in 1498 and visited [[Malindi]], making this the earliest documented Portuguese contact with present-day Kenya.<ref name="kenya1498">{{Cite web|url=https://museums.or.ke/vasco-dagama-pillar/|title=Vasco Da Gama Pillar – National Museums of Kenya}}</ref>
* '''1498:''' {{flagicon|Tanzania}} [[Tanzania]] — Vasco da Gama became the first European recorded to visit the Tanzanian coast when he reached [[Mombasa]] and [[Kilwa Kisiwani]] during his 1498 voyage.<ref name="tanzania1498">{{cite web |url=https://www.visittanzania.org/tanzania-fast-facts/history/ |title=History |date=12 December 2014 |publisher=Visit Tanzania |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1500:''' {{flagicon|Brazil}} [[Brazil]] — [[Pedro Álvares Cabral]] reached the coast of present-day Brazil on April 22, with the fleet making landfall near what is now [[Porto Seguro]] in [[Bahia]]. Cabral's expedition formally took possession of the territory for Portugal, making this the earliest firmly documented European arrival in present-day Brazil.<ref name="brazil1500">{{cite web |url=https://www.gov.br/pt-br/campanhas/bicentenario./linha-do-tempo-da-independencia |title=Linha do Tempo da Independência |publisher=Government of Brazil |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="brazil1500b">{{cite web |url=https://www.gov.br/iphan/pt-br/patrimonio-cultural/patrimonio-material/bens-tombados/conjuntos-urbanos-tombados-cidades-historicas/nordeste/porto-seguro-ba |title=Porto Seguro (BA) |publisher=Instituto do Patrimônio Histórico e Artístico Nacional |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="brazil1500c">{{cite web |url=https://www.gov.br/museugoeldi/pt-br/a-instituicao/difusao-cientifica/publicacao/catalogo-de-publicacoes/os-primeiros-documentos-sobre-a-historia-natural-do-brasil-1500-1511 |title=Os Primeiros Documentos sobre a história natural do Brasil (1500–1511) |publisher=Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1500:''' {{flagicon|Madagascar}} [[Madagascar]] — [[Diogo Dias]] sighted Madagascar on August 10 after being separated from Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet and named it São Lourenço.<ref name="madagascar1500">{{cite web |url=https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/divers/Madagascar_histoire/187014 |title=Madagascar : histoire |publisher=Larousse |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1501:''' {{flagicon|Saint Helena}} [[Ascension Island]] — [[João da Nova]] was the first known human to discover Ascension Island in 1501, initially naming it Conception. [[Afonso de Albuquerque]] encountered it again in 1503 on Ascension Day, giving it the name by which it is now known.<ref name="ascension1501">{{cite web |url=https://www.ascension.gov.ac/section/history |title=A History of Ascension Island |publisher=Ascension Island Government |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1502:''' {{flagicon|Seychelles}} [[Seychelles]] — a Portuguese fleet under Vasco da Gama are the first known humans to record the Seychelles region, during the fourth Portuguese India Armada. [[Thomé Lopes]] recorded the sighting of an elevated island on March 15, 1503, generally identified with [[Silhouette Island]].<ref name="seychelles1502">{{cite web |url=https://www.visitseychelles.org/about-seychelles/history/ |title=History - Visit Seychelles |date=12 May 2020 |publisher=Visit Seychelles |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1502:''' {{flagicon|Saint Helena}} [[Saint Helena]] — João da Nova is credited with being the first human to discover Saint Helena on May 21, during his return voyage from India, although the historical evidence for the precise discovery is disputed.<ref name="sainthelena1502">{{cite web |url=https://www.sainthelena.gov.sh/saint-helena/history/ |title=History |publisher=Government of Saint Helena |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1502:''' {{flagicon|Brazil}} [[Trindade and Martim Vaz]] — João da Nova was the first known human to discover the islands during his 1502 voyage to India; they were subsequently incorporated into Portuguese charts of the South Atlantic.<ref name="trindade1502">{{Cite web| title=Bryological Studies on Trindade Island, South Atlantic | url=https://www.britishbryologicalsociety.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/FB118_Trindade_Bryos-Abroad.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220617212837/https://www.britishbryologicalsociety.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/FB118_Trindade_Bryos-Abroad.pdf | archive-date=2022-06-17}}</ref>
* '''1502–1503:''' {{flagicon|Maldives}} [[Maldives]] — Portuguese fleets reached the Maldives during the early sixteenth-century Portuguese expansion into the Indian Ocean.<ref name="maldives1502">{{Cite web|url=https://maldivians4chagos.com/when-the-mask-falls-fereithaa-foalhavahi-and-the-hidden-maritime-war-in-the-indian-ocean/|title=When the Mask Falls: Fereithaa, Foalhavahi, and the Hidden Maritime War in the Indian Ocean -|date=April 26, 2026}}</ref>
* '''1503:''' {{flagicon|Brazil}} [[Fernando de Noronha]] — [[Amerigo Vespucci]] was the first known human to visit Fernando de Noronha on August 10, 1503, as part of the expedition commanded by [[Gonçalo Coelho]].<ref name="noronha1503">{{cite web |url=https://www.noronha.pe.gov.br/turismo/patrimonio/patrimonio-historico-da-ilha/ |title=Patrimônio Histórico |date=29 April 2022 |publisher=Government of Fernando de Noronha |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1505:''' {{flagicon|Comoros}} [[Comoros]] — Portuguese navigators first visited the Comoros archipelago in 1505 during voyages between East Africa and India.<ref name="comoros1505">{{Cite web|url=https://2009-2017.state.gov/outofdate/bgn/comoros/182224.htm|title=Comoros (10/12/11)|website=U.S. Department of State}}</ref>
* '''1506:''' {{flagicon|Tristan da Cunha}} [[Tristan da Cunha]] — [[Tristão da Cunha]] is the first known human to sight the island in 1506, during a Portuguese voyage toward India; he was unable to land because of rough seas.<ref name="tristan1506">{{Cite web|url=https://www.tristandc.com/history1506-1817.php|title=Tristan da Cunha Discovery & Settlement 1506 - 1817|first=Richard|last=Grundy|website=www.tristandc.com}}</ref>
* '''1511:''' {{flagicon|Mauritius}} [[Mauritius]] — the Portuguese sailor Domingo Fernandez Pereira is considered the first known human to land on Mauritius, around 1511.<ref name="mauritius1511">{{cite web |url=https://www.govmu.org/EN/Pages/exploremauritius.aspx |title=About Mauritius |publisher=Government of Mauritius |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1511–1515:''' {{flagicon|Zimbabwe}} [[Zimbabwe]] — the Portuguese traveler António Fernandes made journeys into the interior of the [[Mutapa]] state in approximately 1511–1515, becoming one of the first Europeans documented in territory of present-day Zimbabwe.<ref name="zimbabwe1511">{{cite web |url=https://www.zimfieldguide.com/sites/mashonaland-central/antonio-fernandes-probably-first-european-traveller-zimbabwe-1511-12 |title=Antonio Fernandes, probably the first European traveller to Zimbabwe in 1511–12 |publisher=Zimbabwe Field Guide |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1512:''' {{flagicon|British Indian Ocean Territory}} [[British Indian Ocean Territory]] — Portuguese captain Pedro de Mascarenhas was the first known human to sight the [[Chagos Archipelago]] and its [[Diego Garcia|largest island]] in February 1512. Mascarenhas named it ''Ilha de Dom Garcia'' after  Dom Garcia de Noronha, who was a financial backer of this specific voyage.<ref name="chagos1512">{{cite web |url=https://ode.govmu.org/ode-data/chagos-archipelago-including-diego-garcia |title=Chagos Archipelago including Diego Garcia |publisher=Government of Mauritius, Observatoire de l'Environnement |access-date=2026-10-18}}</ref><ref name="chagos1512b">{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/museums/seabee/explore/online-reading-room/historic-topics0/diego-garcia.html/1000 |title=Diego Garcia |publisher=United States Navy Seabee Museum |access-date=2026-10-18}}</ref><ref name="chagos1512d">{{cite web |url=https://opendata.uni-halle.de/bitstream/1981185920/8547/1/Johannessen%20PHD.pdf |title=Sacralising the Contested |type=PhD thesis |publisher=Martin Luther University Halle-Wittenberg |access-date=2026-10-18}}</ref>
* '''1512:''' {{flagicon|Indonesia}} [[Indonesia]] — Portuguese expeditions reached the [[Maluku Islands|Moluccas]].<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.worldhistory.org/article/1872/european-discovery--conquest-of-the-spice-islands/|title=European Discovery & Conquest of the Spice Islands|first=James|last=Hancock|date=November 8, 2021|journal=World History Encyclopedia|via=www.worldhistory.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Moluccas|title=Moluccas | Islands, Definition, Map, & History | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref>
* '''1515:''' {{flagicon|Timor-Leste}} [[Timor-Leste]] — the first Europeans to arrive were the Portuguese in 1515.<ref name="timor1599">{{Cite web| title=History - Portuguese Timor | url=https://timor-leste.gov.tl/?p=29&print=1&lang=en | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100530111344/http://timor-leste.gov.tl/?p=29&print=1&lang=en | archive-date=2010-05-30}}</ref>
* '''1516:''' {{flagicon|Argentina}} [[Argentina]] — [[Juan Díaz de Solís]] reached the [[Río de la Plata]] in 1516, making his voyage the earliest documented European exploration of the territory of present-day Argentina.<ref name="argentina1516">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Argentina/History |title=Argentina: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1516:''' {{flagicon|Uruguay}} [[Uruguay]] — Juan Díaz de Solís reached the Río de la Plata and the coast of present-day Uruguay in 1516.<ref name="uruguay1516">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Uruguay/History |title=Uruguay: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1520:''' {{flagicon|Chile}} [[Chile]] — [[Ferdinand Magellan]] passed through the [[Strait of Magellan]].<ref name="chile1520">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Chile/History |title=Chile: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1521:''' {{flagicon|French Polynesia}} [[French Polynesia]] — Ferdinand Magellan's expedition sighted [[Puka-Puka]] in the [[Tuamotu Archipelago]], generally regarded as the first recorded European encounter with the islands now comprising French Polynesia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ferdinand-Magellan/Discovery-of-the-Strait-of-Magellan|title=Ferdinand Magellan - Explorer, Strait, Voyage | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref>
* '''1521:''' {{flagicon|Kiribati}} [[Kiribati]] — Ferdinand Magellan's expedition sighted [[Flint Island]] in the [[Line Islands]], making it the earliest European sighting of territory now belonging to Kiribati.<ref name="kiribati1521">{{Cite web|url=https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p66561/mobile/ch02s07.html|title=The voyage: the Straits and the Ocean—Mactan|website=press-files.anu.edu.au}}</ref>
* '''1524:''' {{flagicon|Paraguay}} [[Paraguay]] — [[Aleixo Garcia]] travelled west from the Atlantic coast with a large [[Guaraní people|Guaraní]] force in 1524 and became the first European known to reach the territory of present-day Paraguay and the site of modern [[Asunción]].<ref name="bolivia1524">{{cite web |url=https://www.asuncion.gov.py/historia-de-mis-calles/una-calle-recuerda-al-portugues-alejo-garcia-que-conocio-paragua-y-trece-anos-antes-de-la-fundacion-de-asuncion |title=Una calle recuerda al portugués Alejo García, que conoció Paraguay trece años antes de la fundación de Asunción |date=18 March 2024 |publisher=Municipalidad de Asunción |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1524–1525:''' {{flagicon|Bolivia}} [[Bolivia]] — Aleixo Garcia and his Guaraní allies crossed the [[Gran Chaco]], with Garcia becoming the first European to encounter the [[Inca Empire]], reaching territory in the vicinity of present-day Bolivia.<ref name="bolivia1524"/>
* '''1526:''' {{flagicon|Ecuador}} [[Ecuador]] — Spanish reconnaissance reached the coast.<ref name="ecuador1526">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Ecuador/History |title=Ecuador: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1526–1527:''' {{flagicon|Indonesia}}{{flagicon|Papua New Guinea}} [[New Guinea]] — [[Jorge de Meneses]] became the first European generally credited with reaching New Guinea when he was blown off course while travelling from Malacca toward the Moluccas. His exact landfall is uncertain and may have been in western New Guinea, now part of Indonesia.<ref name="png1526">{{cite web |url=https://www.dfa.gov.pg/history/ |title=History |date=5 January 2024 |publisher=Department of Foreign Affairs, Papua New Guinea |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="png1526b">{{cite web |url=https://pngcanberra.org/history/ |title=History |publisher=High Commission of the Independent State of Papua New Guinea |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1528:''' {{flagicon|Peru}} [[Peru]] — in April 1528, [[Francisco Pizarro]] and his small band of men reached the northern Peruvian coast near [[Tumbes, Peru|Tumbes]], and encountered the Inca Empire. The local inhabitants welcomed the Spaniards warmly and they reported seeing a sophisticated stone city with an abundance of gold and silver decorations inside the homes of local chiefs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://panamaincontext.com/en/articles/the-desperate-gamble-pizarros-journey-from-panama-to-discover-peru|title=Panama In Context|website=panamaincontext.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tern.post.edu.pe/|title=How Did Francisco Pizarro Get To Peru? The Seven-Year Odyssey|date=February 27, 2026|website=The Andean Post}}</ref>
* '''1535:''' {{flagicon|Galápagos Islands}} [[Galápagos Islands]] — [[Tomás de Berlanga]] became the first known human to land on the islands. He was blown off course while sailing from [[Panama]] toward Peru and reached the Galápagos on March 10. When Berlanga and his men landed on the first island, they found an extremely dry, rocky and apparently uninhabited landscape. They searched desperately for fresh water but initially found none, instead encountering animals such as [[Galápagos tortoise|giant tortoises]]. Berlanga considered the land so barren and stony that little could be cultivated.<ref name="galapagos">{{cite web |url=https://galapagueana.darwinfoundation.org/en/history/hist002.html |title=The discovery |publisher=Charles Darwin Foundation |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1540:''' {{flagicon|Chile}} [[Chiloé Archipelago]] — [[Alonso de Camargo]] became the first Spaniard recorded to sight the coast of Chiloé while travelling toward Peru. [[Francisco de Ulloa]] subsequently explored the archipelago in 1553 and is often regarded as its first European explorer in the more substantial sense.<ref name="chiloe1540">{{cite journal |last1=Urbina c |first1=M. Ximena |title=Expediciones a las costas de la Patagonia occidental en el período colonial |journal=Magallania |year=2013 |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=51–84 |doi=10.4067/S0718-22442013000200002 |url=https://www.scielo.cl/scielo.php?pid=S0718-22442013000200002&script=sci_arttext |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1541–1542:''' {{flagicon|Colombia}} [[Colombia]] — [[Francisco de Orellana]] led the first known European expedition down the entire length of the [[Amazon River]] in 1541–1542, passing through a portion of Colombia in the Southern Hemisphere. European exploration of the Northern Hemisphere portion of Colombia dates back to 1499.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.worldhistory.foundation/uncategorized/rediscovering-ancient-colombias-rich-past/|title=Rediscovering Ancient Colombia's Rich Past – World History Foundation|first=James|last=Wiener}}</ref>
* '''1563:''' {{flagicon|Chile}} [[Desventuradas Islands]] — [[Juan Fernández (explorer)|Juan Fernández]] made the first confirmed human sighting. Some accounts list the sighting as being in 1574 rather than 1563.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstream/1885/114825/2/b13217963.pdf |title=b13217963.pdf |website=Open Research Repository |publisher=Australian National University |access-date=27 May 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308597X21004887|title=The hidden landscape: Maritime cultural heritage of the Salas y Gómez and Nazca ridges with implications for conservation on the high seas|first1=James P.|last1=Delgado|first2=Michael L.|last2=Brennan|first3=Sergio A.|last3=Rapu Haoa|first4=Julianna H.|last4=Rapu Leong|first5=Carlos F.|last5=Gaymer|first6=Diego|last6=Carabias|first7=Emily|last7=Stokes|first8=Daniel|last8=Wagner|date=February 8, 2022|journal=Marine Policy|volume=136|article-number=104877|doi=10.1016/j.marpol.2021.104877 |bibcode=2022MarPo.13604877D }}</ref>
* '''1568:''' {{flagicon|Solomon Islands}} [[Solomon Islands]] and [[Tuvalu]] {{flagicon|Tuvalu}} — [[Álvaro de Mendaña]] reached the islands.<ref name="solomon">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Solomon-Islands/History |title=Solomon Islands: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref><ref name="tuvalu">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Tuvalu/History |title=Tuvalu: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1574:''' {{flagicon|Juan Fernández Islands}} [[Juan Fernández Islands]] — Juan Fernández was the first known human to sight the archipelago on November 22.<ref name="juanfernandez2">{{cite journal |title=Human Impacts on the Vegetation of the Juan Fernández (Robinson Crusoe) Archipelago |journal=Plants |year=2023 |volume=12}}</ref>
* '''1592:''' {{flagicon|Falkland Islands}} [[Falkland Islands]] — [[John Davis (explorer)|John Davis]] sighted the islands in 1592. John Strong made the first recorded landing on the islands in 1690.<ref name="falklands1592">{{cite web |url=https://falklands.gov.fk/our-history-qi83r47ow |title=Our history |publisher=Falkland Islands Government |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1595:''' {{flagicon|Cook Islands}} [[Cook Islands]] — Álvaro de Mendaña reached the islands.<ref name="cookislands">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Cook-Islands/History |title=Cook Islands: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1606:''' {{flagicon|Australia}} [[Australia]] — [[Willem Janszoon]] made the first documented European contact.<ref name="australia65k">{{cite web |url=https://australian.museum/learn/science/archaeology/what-is-the-oldest-evidence-of-people-in-australia/ |title=What is the oldest evidence of people in Australia? |publisher=Australian Museum |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1606:''' {{flagicon|Australia}} [[Torres Strait Islands]] — [[Luís Vaz de Torres]], commanding part of the [[Pedro Fernandes de Queirós]] expedition, sailed through the strait between New Guinea and Australia in 1606, making the first recorded European passage through the region.<ref name="torres1606">{{cite web |url=https://www.alrc.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/fr133_02._context.pdf |title=History of European contact with the Torres Strait |publisher=Australian Law Reform Commission |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="torres1606b">{{cite web |url=https://www.sl.nsw.gov.au/stories/voyages-discovery/plane-sailing |title=Voyages of Discovery: Plane Sailing |publisher=State Library of New South Wales |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1606:''' {{flagicon|Vanuatu}} [[Vanuatu]] — Pedro Fernandes de Queirós reached the islands.<ref name="vanuatu">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Vanuatu/History |title=Vanuatu: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1606:''' {{flagicon|Pitcairn Islands}} [[Pitcairn Islands]] — sighted by Pedro Fernandes de Queirós.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nonnativespecies.org/overseas-territories/territory-pages/pitcairn-islands|title=Pitcairn Islands » NNSS|website=www.nonnativespecies.org}}</ref>
* '''1609:''' {{flagicon|Cocos (Keeling) Islands}} [[Cocos (Keeling) Islands]] — [[William Keeling]] became the first known human to discover the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, while returning from the East Indies.<ref name="cocoskeeling1609">{{cite web |url=https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-observatory/south-keeling-atoll-152930/ |title=South Keeling Atoll |date=16 June 2024 |publisher=NASA Earth Observatory |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1616:''' {{flagicon|Malawi}} [[Malawi]] — Gaspar Bocarro travelled overland from [[Tete, Mozambique]] to [[Kilwa]] in 1616, producing the earliest substantial European written account referring to the territory around the southern end of [[Lake Malawi]]. His journey is treated in scholarly literature as the beginning of the written European record for the country.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Hamilton | first1=R. A. | title=The Route of Gaspar Bocarro from Tete to Kilwa in 1616 | journal=The Nyasaland Journal | date=1954 | volume=7 | issue=2 | pages=7–14 | jstor=29545718 | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/29545718 }}</ref>
* '''1616:''' {{flagicon|Tonga}} [[Tonga]] — [[Willem Schouten]] and [[Jacob Le Maire]] reached Tonga in 1616 and 1643.<ref name="tonga">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Tonga/History |title=Tonga: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1616:''' {{flagicon|Wallis and Futuna}} [[Wallis and Futuna]] — Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire reached the islands.<ref name="wallis">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Wallis-and-Futuna |title=Wallis and Futuna |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1642:''' {{flagicon|New Zealand}} [[New Zealand]] — [[Abel Tasman]] made the first firm documented European sighting.<ref name="nz">{{cite web |url=https://nzhistory.govt.nz/page/european-voyaging-and-discovery |title=European voyaging and discovery |publisher=New Zealand History, Ministry for Culture and Heritage |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1642:''' {{flagicon|Tasmania}} [[Tasmania]] — [[Abel Tasman]] sighted and mapped the island.<ref name="tasmania40k">{{cite web |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/the-black-line |title=The Black Line |publisher=National Museum of Australia |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1643:''' {{flagicon|Christmas Island}} [[Christmas Island (Australia)|Christmas Island]] — [[William Mynors]], master of the [[English East India Company]] vessel ''Royal Mary'', was the first known human to sight the island on December 25, 1643. He named it Christmas Island after the day of the sighting. The first recorded landing occurred in 1688, when [[William Dampier]] and members of the crew of the ''Cygnet'' went ashore and found the island uninhabited.<ref name="christmasisland1643">{{cite web |url=https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/territories-regions/territories/indian-ocean-territories-christmas-island-and-cocos-keeling-islands/christmas-island/christmas-island-environment-and-heritage |title=Christmas Island environment and heritage |publisher=Australian Government Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="christmasisland1643b">{{cite web |url=https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/sites/default/files/migrated/territories/publications/files/A_Federation_in_These_Seas_Part_3.pdf |title=A Federation in These Seas: An account of the external territories |publisher=Australian Government |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1643:''' {{flagicon|Fiji}} [[Fiji]] — [[Abel Tasman]] reached the islands.<ref name="fiji">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Fiji-republic-Pacific-Ocean/History |title=Fiji: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1675:''' {{flagicon|South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands}} [[South Georgia]] — [[Anthony de la Roché]] is traditionally credited with being the first human to discover South Georgia in April 1675, although modern scholarship questions both his identity and whether the island he saw was actually South Georgia. [[James Cook]] made the first undisputed landing and detailed survey in 1775.<ref name="southgeorgia1675">{{cite journal |last=Campbell |first=Gordon |title=Antonio de la Roche and the discovery of South Georgia |journal=Polar Record |year=2023 |doi=10.1017/S0032247423000202 |doi-broken-date=10 September 2026 }}</ref><ref name="southgeorgia1675b">{{cite web |url=https://www.gov.gs/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Main-Report-July-2011.pdf |title=Appendix 2: Timeline |publisher=Government of South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1722:''' {{flagicon|Easter Island}} [[Easter Island]] — [[Jacob Roggeveen]] reached the island, and noted that it was inhabited and had numerous [[Moai|large stone heads]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/77886/77886-h/77886-h.htm|title=An historical account of all the voyages round the world, performed by English navigators. (Volume 1 of 4) | Project Gutenberg|website=www.gutenberg.org}}</ref>{{AI-retrieved source|date=September 2026|checked=September 2026}}<ref name="rapanui">{{cite web |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/715/ |title=Rapa Nui National Park |publisher=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ebsco.com/|title=European Discovery of Easter Island | History | Research Starters | EBSCOhost|website=EBSCO}}</ref>
* '''1722:''' {{flagicon|American Samoa}} [[American Samoa]] and {{flagicon|Samoa}} [[Samoa]] — Jacob Roggeveen reached the Samoan islands.<ref name="samoa">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Samoa-island-nation-Pacific-Ocean/History |title=Samoa: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1739:''' {{flagicon|Bouvet Island}} [[Bouvet Island]] — [[Jean-Baptiste Charles Bouvet de Lozier]] was the first known human to discover the island on January 1, 1739. He promptly lost the location of the island as he did not chart it correctly. This prevented others from reaching the island again until the early 19th century. It was so far away from Bouvet's reported position, though, that those who saw it thought it was a completely different island.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Bouvet-Island|title=Bouvet Island | Map, History, & Facts | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://utmsi.utexas.edu/science-and-the-sea/radio-program/bouvet-island/|title=Bouvet Island}}</ref>
* '''1765:''' {{flagicon|Tokelau}} [[Tokelau]] — [[John Byron]] reached the islands.<ref name="tokelau">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Tokelau |title=Tokelau |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1767:''' {{flagicon|Tahiti}} [[Tahiti]] — [[Samuel Wallis]] aboard HMS ''Dolphin'' made the first European visit to Tahiti, arriving off the island on June 19 and anchoring at [[Matavai Bay]]. Wallis named it ''King George III Island''.<ref name="tahiti1767">{{cite web |url=https://natlib.govt.nz/records/22353140 |title=Samuel Wallis: King George III Island, June 26 1767 |publisher=National Library of New Zealand |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref><ref name="tahiti1767b">{{cite web |url=https://www.nma.gov.au/explore/features/cook_forster/background/collectors |title=Collectors — First exchanges |publisher=National Museum of Australia |access-date=2026-09-09}}</ref>
* '''1772:''' {{flagicon|French Southern and Antarctic Lands}} [[Kerguelen Islands]] — [[Yves-Joseph de Kerguelen-Trémarec]] was the first known human to discover the archipelago on February 12, 1772, and named it France Australe.<ref name="kerguelen1772">{{cite web |url=https://rdf.archives-nationales.culture.gouv.fr/garance/entities/agent/001917 |title=Kerguelen |publisher=Archives nationales de France |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1774:''' {{flagicon|New Caledonia}} [[New Caledonia]] — James Cook sighted the island.<ref name="newcaledonia">{{cite web |url=https://www.britannica.com/place/New-Caledonia/History |title=New Caledonia: History |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1774:''' {{flagicon|Niue}} [[Niue]] — James Cook made the first documented European landing on Niue during his second Pacific voyage in 1774.<ref name="niue1774">{{cite web |url=https://gov.nu/our-history |title=Our History |publisher=Government of Niue |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1774:''' {{flagicon|Norfolk Island}} [[Norfolk Island]] — James Cook sighted and landed on the island.<ref name="norfolk">{{cite web |url=https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/territories-regions-cities/territories/norfolk-island/history |title=Norfolk Island history and heritage |publisher=Australian Government |access-date=2026-09-07}}</ref>
* '''1775:''' {{flagicon|South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands}} [[South Sandwich Islands]] — James Cook is the first known human to discover the South Sandwich Islands during his second voyage in 1775, sighting eight rocky masses through fog and snow. Cook did not land, and he initially could not determine whether all the features were separate islands. The northern three islands of the group were later discovered by [[Fabian Gottlieb von Bellingshausen|Fabian von Bellingshausen]] in 1819, who also confirmed the islands seen by Cook.<ref name="southsandwich1775">{{cite web |url=https://gov.gs/south-sandwich-islands-stamp-release/ |title=South Sandwich Islands Stamp Release |date=29 June 2026 |publisher=Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref><ref name="southsandwich1775b">{{cite pdf |url=https://gov.gs/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/SGSSI-Heritage-Framework-and-Strategy.pdf |title=Heritage Framework and Strategy |publisher=Government of South Georgia & the South Sandwich Islands |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
* '''1788:''' {{flagicon|Australia}} [[Coral Sea Islands]] — [[John Shortland]] discovered [[Middleton Reef]] on July 20 while returning from Australia to [[Batavia, Dutch East Indies|Batavia]]. The broader Coral Sea Islands and reefs were subsequently charted by numerous European navigators.<ref name="coralsea1788">{{cite web |url=https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/territories-regions/territories/coral-sea-islands |title=Coral Sea Islands |publisher=Australian Government Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications and the Arts |access-date=2026-09-08}}</ref>
