== Laws and legal systems ==

The Southern Hemisphere has no common legal system, with countries using [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]], [[common law]], [[customary law]], [[Islamic law]] and hybrid systems. Road-traffic rules are an example of some of the historical differences. Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru and Uruguay drive on the right, as do several mainland African states. Most former British territories in southern and eastern Africa drive on the left, as do many insular states in the South Atlantic, South Pacific and Indian Ocean, including Australia, as most of these states are also former British territories.<ref name="driving-side">RAC, "[https://www.rac.co.uk/drive/travel/advice/driving-on-the-left-or-right-across-the-world/ Driving on the left or right – a global guide]", 22 June 2026.</ref> Left-hand traffic is strongly associated with British and regional colonial practice, but is not confined to former British possessions: Mozambique, formerly Portuguese, drives on the left as part of the southern African road system. Indonesia and Timor-Leste also do so, as does the Northern Hemisphere country Japan, reflecting a broader trend of island countries driving on the left. The island countries Samoa and Vanuatu were exceptions to this trend, as Samoa was formerly a German colony, while Vanuatu was jointly administered by France and the United Kingdom. Samoa changed from right to left-hand traffic on September 7, 2009, making it a notable example of a deliberate modern change in road law.<ref name="samoa-traffic">{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/sep/08/samoa-drivers-switch-left|title=Samoa switches smoothly to driving on the left|first=Associated|last=Press|work=The Guardian |date=September 8, 2009}}</ref>

The Falkland Islands illustrate the separate legal status that some overseas territories possess. As a British Overseas Territory, they have their own Constitution, Legislative Assembly, courts and local laws; United Kingdom legislation applies only where extended or otherwise applicable, while English common law and equity apply subject to local legislation.<ref name="falklands-law">Falkland Islands Government, ''Falkland Islands Statute Law Database'' and ''Law Revision and Publication Ordinance 2017''. [https://www.falklands.gov.fk/legalservices/statute-law-commissioner/falklands-islands-statute-law-database] [https://www.legislation.gov.fk/view/lh/inforce/current/fiord-2017-11]</ref> During the [[Falklands War]], Argentina occupied the islands from April to June 1982, and Argentine authorities temporarily ordered vehicles to drive on the right instead of the Islands' normal left-hand system. The Islands reverted to left-hand traffic after the end of the occupation.<ref name="twenty">{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/theobserver/2002/mar/17/features.magazine37|title=Oh! What a lovely war|first=Anthony|last=Browne|work=The Guardian |date=March 17, 2002}}</ref>

Other Southern Hemisphere territories have varying degrees of legal autonomy from their metropolitan states, including the Pitcairn Islands, [[Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha]], French Polynesia, New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, American Samoa, the Cook Islands, Niue and Tokelau. In Tokelau, New Zealand statutes do not automatically apply unless extended, while village rules, General Fono rules and Tokelau's constitutional arrangements form part of its legal order.<ref name="tokelau-law">Government of Tokelau, ''Government – Law'' and ''Constitution of Tokelau''. [https://www.tokelau.org.nz/About%2BUs/Government.html] [https://www.tokelau.org.nz/About%2BUs/Government/Self%2BDetermination%2BPackage/Constitution%2Bof%2BTokelau.html]</ref> Cook Islands and Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand and have their own constitutions and domestic legislation.<ref name="cook-niue">New Zealand Legislation, ''Cook Islands Constitution Act 1964''; Government of Niue, information on self-government in free association with New Zealand. [https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1964/69/en/latest/] [https://www.gov.nu/government]</ref> Norfolk Island, meanwhile, has undergone increasing integration into Australia's federal legal and administrative system since reforms beginning in the 2010s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5445|title=Tax and Superannuation Laws Amendment (Norfolk Island Reforms) Bill 2015|first=Canberra|last=corporateName=Commonwealth Parliament; address=Parliament House|publisher=corporateName=Commonwealth Parliament; address=Parliament House, Canberra, ACT, 2600; contact=+61 2 6277 7111|website=www.aph.gov.au}}</ref> Tokelau is excluded from the [[Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership]] (CPTPP), a trade agreement among various Pacific Rim countries. By contrast, Australia's territories Christmas Island, Cocos (Keeling) Islands, Heard Island and McDonald Islands and Norfolk Island are not excluded from the CPTPP's geographic scope.<ref name="cptpp-abf">Australian Border Force, ''Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) Rules of Origin'', noting the original 11 parties and defining the geographical area covered by the agreement; for New Zealand, the agreement expressly ''does not include Tokelau''. [https://www.abf.gov.au/free-trade-agreements/files/tpp-11-importers-guide.pdf]</ref>

=== Criminalization of consensual same-sex sexual activity ===

Legal treatment of same-sex conduct varies substantially. As of April 30, 2024, [[International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association|ILGA World]] identified 62 United Nations member states that criminalized consensual same-sex sexual activity in law or practice. Many of these are Islamic countries in the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="ilga-2024">{{cite web | title=Laws on Us: A global overview of legal progress and backtracking on SOGIESC | website=ILGA World | date=May 30, 2024 | url=https://ilga.org/resources/laws-on-us-global-overview-2024/ | access-date=October 13, 2026}}</ref> Consensual same-sex sexual activity remains criminalized in the Southern Hemisphere countries Burundi, Comoros, Eswatini, Kenya, Malawi, Maldives, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Somalia, Tanzania, Tonga, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe.<ref name="ilga-criminalising">{{Cite web|url=https://ilga.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Laws_On_Us_2024.pdf|title=ILGA World, ''Laws on Us'' (2024)}}</ref> Burundi provides imprisonment of up to two years, while the Islamic nation Comoros provides imprisonment and fines for same-sex sexual conduct under its Penal Code.<ref name="burundi-sexual">{{Cite web|url=https://www.socialscienceinaction.org/resources/supporting-the-mpox-response-for-people-with-diverse-sexual-orientation-gender-identity-and-or-gender-expression-in-contexts-where-their-rights-are-restricted/|title=Supporting the mpox response for people with diverse sexual orientation, gender identity and/or gender expression in contexts where their rights are restricted}}</ref><ref name="comoros-sexual">ILGA World, ''Our Identities under Arrest''; United States Department of State, country material on Comoros. [https://www.ilga.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Our_Identities_Under_Arrest_2023.pdf] [https://2021-2025.state.gov/reports/2023-country-reports-on-human-rights-practices/comoros/]</ref>

Kenya criminalizes consensual same-sex sexual activity between men, with penalties of up to 14 years under section 162 of the Penal Code, while Malawi and Zambia also retain criminal prohibitions.<ref name="kenya-sexual">{{Cite web|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/kenya-country-policy-and-information-notes/country-policy-and-information-note-sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity-and-expression-kenya-february-2025-accessible|title=Country policy and information note: sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, Kenya, February 2025 (accessible)|website=GOV.UK}}</ref><ref name="malawi-sexual">{{Cite web|url=https://www.humandignitytrust.org./country-profile/malawi/|title=Malawi|date=December 16, 2024}}</ref><ref name="zambia-sexual">{{Cite web|url=https://zambialii.org/akn/zm/act/1930/42/eng@2023-12-26|title=Penal Code, 1930|date=December 26, 2023}}</ref> Uganda is particularly restrictive: its Anti-Homosexuality Act provides severe penalties, including the [[death penalty]] for certain cases of “aggravated homosexuality”.<ref name="uganda-sexual">{{Cite web|url=https://ilga.org/news/uganda-ilga-world-pan-africa-ilga-anti-homosexuality-act/|title=Uganda: ILGA World and Pan Africa ILGA condemn Court ruling to uphold Anti-Homosexuality Act|date=April 5, 2024}}</ref>

Despite being a majority Islamic country, Indonesia does not generally criminalize consensual same-sex activity at the national level solely because it is same-sex. Indonesia's [[Aceh]], which is above the equator, applies Islamic criminal law to same-sex acts. Some local regulations impose additional restrictions.<ref name="indonesia-sexual">ILGA World, ''Laws on Us'' (2024), and ''Our Identities under Arrest'' (2023). [https://ilga.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Laws_On_Us_2024.pdf]</ref>

South Africa decriminalized consensual same-sex sexual activity in 1998.<ref name="ilga-2024"/> Since 2012, Angola, Botswana, Lesotho, Mauritius, Mozambique, Nauru, Seychelles and São Tomé and Príncipe have also decriminalized consensual same-sex sexual activity.<ref name="ilga-2024"/> In June 2024, Namibia's High Court struck down colonial-era laws criminalizing sex between men, but the government appealed.<ref name="namibia">Government of the United Kingdom, ''Country information and guidance: Sexual orientation and gender identity and expression in Namibia'', October 2024. [https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/namibia-country-policy-and-information-notes/country-information-and-guidance-sexual-orientation-and-gender-identity-and-expression-in-namibia-accessible-version]</ref>

=== Death penalty ===

The usage of the death penalty also varies considerably in the Southern Hemisphere. [[Amnesty International]] classified countries (as of December 31, 2025) according to whether capital punishment was abolished, retained only for exceptional offences, abolished in practice or retained for ordinary crimes.<ref name="amnesty-2025">Amnesty International, ''Death Sentences and Executions 2025'', Annex II. [https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ACT5007782026ENGLISH.pdf]</ref> Among Southern Hemisphere countries, capital punishment is abolished for all crimes in Angola, Argentina, Australia, Bolivia, Burundi, Colombia, Republic of the Congo, Ecuador, Gabon, Madagascar, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Nauru, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Rwanda, São Tomé and Príncipe, Seychelles, Solomon Islands, South Africa, Timor-Leste, Tuvalu, Uruguay, Vanuatu and Zambia.<ref name="amnesty-2025" /> Brazil, Chile, Equatorial Guinea, Peru and Zimbabwe retain it only for exceptional offences, while Eswatini, Kenya, Malawi, Maldives, Tanzania and Tonga are abolitionist in practice. Botswana, Comoros, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Lesotho, Somalia and Uganda retain the death penalty for ordinary crimes.<ref name="amnesty-2025" /> Amnesty recorded executions in Somalia in 2025, while death sentences were also recorded in several other retentionist states.<ref name="amnesty-2025-executions">Amnesty International, ''Death Sentences and Executions 2025'', Annex I. [https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/ACT5007782026ENGLISH.pdf]</ref> Australia abolished capital punishment federally in 1973 and progressively removed it from state and territory law, making it fully abolitionist.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sbs.com.au/language/arabic/en/article/in-what-year-did-the-federal-government-abolish-capital-punishment/v5u2q0hwe|title=In What year did the Federal Government abolish Capital Punishment?|date=February 28, 2017|website=SBS Language}}</ref>

=== Penal systems ===
Penal systems across the Southern Hemisphere vary according to each country's legal system, population and resources. Several operate a combination of remand facilities, sentenced prisons and different security classifications, ranging from minimum or open custody to medium, high and maximum security. For example, South Africa formally classifies sentenced prisoners as minimum, medium or maximum security according to assessed security risk, while Australia likewise uses multiple classification levels, including maximum-security categories.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is security classification of inmates? |url=https://www.dcs.gov.za/?accordion_tp=what-is-security-classification-of-inmates |publisher=South African Department of Correctional Services |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Classification and Placement |url=https://correctiveservices.dcj.nsw.gov.au/documents/csnsw-fact-sheets/classification-and-placement.pdf |publisher=Corrective Services NSW |date=2026 |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Under Brazil's 1984 Lei de Execução Penal law, convicted prisoners are theoretically divided among closed, semi-open and open regimes, with progression toward less restrictive conditions intended as part of the rehabilitation process.<ref>{{Cite web | title=HRW: Behind Bars in Brazil (Overview of the System) | url=https://www.hrw.org/legacy/reports98/brazil/Brazil-03.htm | access-date=2026-09-11 | website=www.hrw.org}}</ref> Arrangements for women vary especially widely between countries because female prison populations are generally much smaller than male populations: some countries operate dedicated women's prisons, while others accommodate women in separate sections or units within larger mixed or primarily male correctional complexes. New Zealand, for example, operates three dedicated women's prisons, while in Australia both dedicated women's facilities and prisons containing separate male and female units exist.<ref>{{cite web |title=Women in prison |url=https://www.corrections.govt.nz/homepage_redev_2019/homepage_main_listing/in_prison/being_in_prison/women_in_prison |publisher=Department of Corrections New Zealand |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Prison Institutions |url=https://lsc.sa.gov.au/handbook/ch33s02s01.php |publisher=Legal Services Commission of South Australia |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Brazil legally requires women to be held separately from men and also prohibits women's prisons from using male guards.<ref>{{Cite web | title=Brazil's Illegal Treatment of Women in Prison {{!}} Human Rights Watch | url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2017/03/06/brazils-illegal-treatment-women-prison | access-date=2026-09-11 | website=www.hrw.org}}</ref>

Penal systems in the Southern Hemisphere have also been strongly influenced by colonial history, with several territories in the South Pacific becoming particularly associated with [[penal colony|penal transportation]], exile and forced labour. Australia is the most prominent example: from 1787 to 1868, Britain transported about 166,000 men, women and children to its Australian colonies, where convict settlements combined imprisonment and punishment with forced labour and colonial development. The system included mainland sites as well as isolated locations such as Norfolk Island and Tasmania, with distance from Britain and the difficulty of escape making transportation itself part of the punishment.<ref>{{cite web |title=Australian Convict Sites |url=https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1306/ |publisher=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> Norfolk Island was particularly notorious as a place for secondary punishment, being described as an "ultimate deterrent" for convicts considered unlikely to reform.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fremantle Prison Conservation Management Plan |url=https://whc.unesco.org/document/105329 |publisher=UNESCO World Heritage Centre |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> This use of geographic isolation was not unique to Australia; neighboring New Caledonia, then already a French territory, operated as a major penal colony from 1864, receiving more than 22,000 French convicts between 1864 and 1897, including approximately 4,500 political prisoners associated with the [[Paris Commune]]. Prisoners were transported to remote island settlements including Île Nou, the Ducos Peninsula and the [[Île des Pins]], where penal labour also contributed to French colonial development.<ref>{{cite web |title=New Caledonia (1864–97) |url=https://www.dcceew.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/convict-sites-part9.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

On the other side of the South Pacific, the Juan Fernández Islands of Chile were also used for confinement and exile, most notably on [[Más a Tierra]] (now known as Robinson Crusoe Island). Chile established a prison settlement on the island in the 19th century, and its extreme isolation made escape difficult, with this being an important reason for its use as a penal site.<ref>{{cite web |title=Isla Robinson Crusoe |url=https://www.monumentos.gob.cl/monumentos/monumentos-historicos/isla-robinson-crusoe |publisher=Consejo de Monumentos Nacionales de Chile |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref> The Galápagos Islands of Ecuador similarly had a history of penal settlements, particularly on Isabela Island, where the Ecuadorian state established the [[Wall of Tears]] and its associated penal colony in the mid-20th century. Ecuador had been experimenting with using the islands as prisons as far back as the 1830s, when they first became part of the country. The islands' distance from the Ecuadorian mainland contributed to their suitability for exile and confinement.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Wall of Tears |url=https://www.galapagos.gob.ec/ |publisher=Dirección del Parque Nacional Galápagos |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

=== Indigenous laws and policies ===

Indigenous land law has continuing significance across much of the Southern Hemisphere. In Australia, [[Mabo v Queensland (No 2)]] (1992) rejected the application of ''[[terra nullius]]'' and recognised [[native title]] arising from the traditional laws and customs of Aboriginal and [[Torres Strait Islander]] peoples.<ref name="mabo">[[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies|AIATSIS]], material on ''Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23''. [https://aiatsis.gov.au/ntpd-resource/742]</ref> The decision led to the [[Native Title Act 1993]], which established a national statutory framework for recognizing and protecting native title.<ref name="nta">Australian Government, Federal Register of Legislation, ''Native Title Act 1993'' (Cth). [https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A04665/]</ref> In New Zealand, Māori land law is shaped by [[Te Tiriti o Waitangi|Te Tiriti o Waitangi / Treaty of Waitangi]] and the [[Te Ture Whenua Māori Act 1993]], which recognises Māori customary and Māori freehold land.<ref name="treaty">{{Cite web|url=https://www.justice.govt.nz/about/learn-about-the-justice-system/how-the-justice-system-works/the-basis-for-all-law/treaty-of-waitangi/|title=Te Tiriti o Waitangi - Treaty of Waitangi|date=September 6, 2025|website=New Zealand Ministry of Justice}}</ref><ref name="maori-land">{{Cite web |date=2026-04-30 |title=Te Ture Whenua Maori Act 1993 |url=https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1993/4/en/latest/sections/DLM291287/ |website=Te Tari Tohutohu Pāremata - Parliamentary Council Office of New Zealand}}</ref> In Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru, constitutional or statutory systems likewise recognise various forms of Indigenous, communal or customary territorial rights.<ref name="indigenous-americas">United Nations, ''United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples'', particularly articles 25–32. [https://www.un.org/development/desa/indigenouspeoples/declaration-on-the-rights-of-indigenous-peoples.html]</ref> Australia, Chile and New Zealand are all members of the CPTPP, and in 2025 they created a pact in the organization called the Birrarung Statement, which aims to increase Indigenous participation in trade activity. The pact was named after Melbourne's [[Yarra River]] (indigenously known as Birrarung) and also included the Northern Hemisphere Pacific Rim countries Canada and [[Mexico]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dfat.gov.au/trade/agreements/in-force/cptpp/background-documents/birrarung-statement|title=The Birrarung Statement|website=Dfat.gov.au|access-date=20 July 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-11-27 |title=The Birrarung Statement |url=https://www.international.gc.ca/trade-commerce/trade-agreements-accords-commerciaux/agr-acc/cptpp-ptpgp/2025-11-27-birrarung.aspx?lang=eng |access-date=2026-03-10 |website=Government of Canada}}</ref>

=== Environmental law ===

In Australia, environmental regulation is divided among Commonwealth, state and territory governments. The [[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]] protects matters of national environmental significance, including [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage]] properties and the [[Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area]], while the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act 1975 establishes the [[Great Barrier Reef Marine Park]] and the [[Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority]].<ref name="epbc-gbr">Australian Government Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, ''EPBC Act referral guidelines for the Outstanding Universal Value of the Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area''. [https://www.dcceew.gov.au/environment/epbc/publications/epbc-act-referral-guidelines-outstanding-universal-value-great-barrier-reef-world-heritage]</ref><ref name="gbrmpa-act">[https://www.gbrmpa.gov.au/about-us/legislation-and-polices/Legislation Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, ''Legislation'']</ref> The Marine Park is a multiple-use protected area divided into zones with different rules for fishing, tourism, research and other activities.<ref name="gbr-zoning">Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, ''How Marine Park Zoning works''. [https://www.gbrmpa.gov.au/access/zoning/how-it-works]</ref> The Reef's World Heritage Site status adds an international conservation framework, and management increasingly incorporates [[Traditional Owners]] and traditional knowledge.<ref name="gbr-worldheritage">Australian Government Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water, ''Great Barrier Reef World Heritage Area''. [https://www.dcceew.gov.au/parks-heritage/great-barrier-reef/world-heritage]</ref>

The Galápagos Islands are their own distinct political province of Ecuador. Due to their high biodiversity, they are subject to a special legal regime concerning settlement, development, tourism and biosecurity.<ref name="galapagos-law">UNESCO World Heritage Centre, ''Special Regime Law for the Preservation and Sustainable Development of the Province of Galapagos''. [https://whc.unesco.org/archive/ecu-gal.pdf]</ref><ref name="galapagos-park">Dirección del Parque Nacional Galápagos, material on the Galápagos National Park. [https://galapagos.gob.ec/parque-nacional-galapagos/]</ref> Galápagos forms part of the Eastern Tropical Pacific Marine Corridor, a regional conservation framework linking Ecuador with Colombia, [[Costa Rica]] and Panama and connecting Galápagos with other eastern Pacific islands including [[Gorgona Island (Colombia)|Gorgona Island]], [[Malpelo Island]], [[Cocos Island]] and [[Coiba Island]] (all of which are above the equator).<ref name="cmar">Corredor Marino del Pacífico Este Tropical (CMAR), material on the corridor and its protected areas. [https://www.cmarpacifico.org/quienes-somos/que-es-el-cmar]</ref>

The [[Amazon rainforest]] in South America is governed by the domestic environmental laws of Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and the Northern Hemisphere countries [[Guyana]], [[Suriname]] and [[Venezuela]]. These countries engage in regional cooperation under the [[Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization]] (ACTO).<ref name="acta">Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), ''How We Work'', describing cooperation among the eight Amazonian countries on sustainability, conservation and management of Amazon territories. [https://otca.org/en/how-we-work/]</ref> Brazil, which contains most of the Amazon biome, has particularly extensive forest protections under its Forest Code (Law No. 12,651/2012), including mandatory Legal Reserve areas on rural properties. In much of the Brazilian Amazon Legal region, rural properties in forest areas must maintain at least 80% of their area as native vegetation, alongside Permanent Preservation Areas protecting features such as riverbanks and springs.<ref name="brazil-forest-code">Brazilian Senate, ''Law No. 12,651/2012 (Forest Code)'', Article 12 and related provisions. [https://legis.senado.gov.br/norma/589574/publicacao/34619111]</ref>

==Historical events==
Most of earth's major conflicts and historical events have occurred in the Northern Hemisphere, where the majority of the world's population, historically important civilizations, and major centres of political power have been concentrated.<ref>Boehmer, Elleke. ''Southern Imagining: A Literary and Cultural History of the Far Southern Hemisphere''. United States, Princeton University Press, 2025.</ref> Conflicts that have taken place entirely or partly south of the equator include the [[Anglo-Zulu War]] (1879), the [[First Boer War]] (1880–1881), the [[Second Boer War]] (1899–1902), the [[East African campaign (World War I)|First World War campaigns in German South West Africa and German East Africa]], the [[Argentine War of Independence]] (1810–1818), the [[Paraguayan War]] (1864–1870), the South American [[War of the Pacific]] (1879–1884), the [[Chaco War]] (1932–1935), the [[Angolan War of Independence]] (1961–1974), the [[Mozambican War of Independence]] (1964–1974), the [[South African Border War]] (1966–1990), the [[Mozambican Civil War]] (1977–1992), the [[Angolan Civil War]] (1975–2002), the Falklands War (1982), the [[First Congo War]] (1996–1997), the [[Second Congo War]] (1998–2003), and the [[Rwandan genocide]] (1994). During the [[Second World War]], major campaigns and battles were also fought in the South Pacific, including the Japanese conquest of the [[Dutch East Indies]] (now Indonesia), the [[Battle of the Coral Sea]], the [[Guadalcanal campaign]] and the [[Kokoda Track campaign]].<ref>{{Cite web | title=Battle of Guadalcanal and Australia - Anzac Portal | url=https://anzacportal.dva.gov.au/wars-and-missions/ww2/where/swpa/guadalcanal-1942-1943 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260508151507/https://anzacportal.dva.gov.au/wars-and-missions/ww2/where/swpa/guadalcanal-1942-1943 | access-date=2026-08-28 | archive-date=2026-05-08}}</ref> Other major non-war events include [[Charles Darwin]]'s 1835 visit to the Galápagos Islands, which helped form the [[theory of evolution]], the first release of [[Nelson Mandela]] from prison on 11 February 1990, a key moment in the eventual end of [[apartheid]] in South Africa; French nuclear weapons testing in French Polynesia between 1966 and 1996; and the 1974 "[[Rumble in the Jungle]]" boxing match between [[Muhammad Ali]] and [[George Foreman]], held in Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (then [[Zaire]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nelsonmandela.org/news/entry/nelson-mandelas-release-from-prison-36-years-on|title=Nelson Mandela's release from prison: 36 years on – Nelson Mandela Foundation|website=www.nelsonmandela.org}}</ref>

The Southern Hemisphere has hosted several FIFA World Cups and [[List of FIFA World Cup finals|FIFA World Cup finals]], including the inaugural tournament in Uruguay in [[1930 FIFA World Cup|1930]], Brazil in [[1950 FIFA World Cup|1950]] and [[2014 FIFA World Cup|2014]], Chile in [[1962 FIFA World Cup|1962]], Argentina in [[1978 FIFA World Cup|1978]], and South Africa in [[2010 FIFA World Cup|2010]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/sports/FIFA-World-Cup-Records|title=FIFA World Cup Records | All-Time Stats, Winners List, Top Goal Scorers, Most Titles, Timeline, Players, Achievements, Awards, & Countries | Britannica|date=July 29, 2026|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref> Over the tournament's history, three Southern Hemisphere countries (Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay) have lifted the trophy on multiple occasions, while Brazil is the only country in the world to have qualified for every edition since 1930.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/sports/Which-National-Teams-Have-Participated-in-the-FIFA-World-Cup|title=Which National Teams Have Participated in the FIFA World Cup? | List, Winners, History, Countries, & Facts | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref> The other Southern Hemisphere countries which have appeared at the tournament since 1930 are Angola, Australia, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (as both Zaire and their current name) Ecuador, Indonesia (as Dutch East Indies), New Zealand, Peru and South Africa. The [[1956 Summer Olympics]] in Melbourne were the first to be held in the Southern Hemisphere. Subsequent editions have been held in Australia, including Sydney in [[2000 Summer Olympics|2000]], and the upcoming [[2032 Summer Olympics|2032]] Games in Brisbane, making Australia one of the few countries to host the Summer Olympic Games across three different cities.  At the [[2002 Winter Olympics]], Australian speed skater [[Steven Bradbury]] won the Southern Hemisphere's first-ever Winter Olympic gold medal in the 1,000m short-track event. Trailing in last place during the final lap, Bradbury watched as all four competitors ahead of him crashed into each other on the final bend. He glided across the finish line untouched to claim gold. This event birthed the Australian [[idiom]] "doing a Bradbury", which refers to achieving unexpected success simply by staying on one's feet while the competition collapses.<ref>{{Cite web | title=The 10 greatest moments in Australian sporting history | url=https://www.espn.com.au/espn/story/_/id/28955820/the-10-greatest-moments-australian-sporting-history | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200408000502/https://www.espn.com.au/espn/story/_/id/28955820/the-10-greatest-moments-australian-sporting-history | access-date=2026-08-28 | archive-date=2020-04-08}}</ref> [[Cadel Evans]], an Australian cyclist born in [[Katherine, Northern Territory]], was the first person from the Southern Hemisphere to win the [[Tour De France]] in [[2011 Tour de France|2011]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-09-26/cadel-evans3a-grinding-his-way-into-history/5770340|title=Cadel Evans: Grinding his way into history|work=ABC News |date=September 25, 2014|via=www.abc.net.au}}</ref> The race was subsequently won by Colombian [[Egan Bernal]] in [[2018 Tour de France|2018]], who became the first Latin American to win, although Bernal was born in a part of Colombia which is above the equator.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2773157X25000906|title=Polytrauma in a professional cyclist: A successful case of timely management, rehabilitation, and rapid return to high-level competition|first1=Juan Guillermo|last1=Ortiz Martínez|first2=Pablo Ricardo|last2=Patarroyo Perea|first3=Bettina Eugenia|last3=Sotillo Gómez|first4=Edgar Manuel|last4=Bodu Lamberti|first5=Camila Karduss|last5=Preciado|first6=Juan Miguel|last6=Molano Díaz|first7=Maria Juliana|last7=Neira Barrero|first8=Angela María|last8=Rico Avendaño|date=September 1, 2025|journal=Journal of Orthopaedic Reports|volume=4|issue=3|pages=100638|via=ScienceDirect|doi=10.1016/j.jorep.2025.100638}}</ref>

By death toll, the worst [[List of major terrorist incidents|terrorist]] incident to have ever occurred in the Southern Hemisphere is the [[2001 Angola train attack]], which was part of the country's civil war and killed 252 people. Other major terrorist incidents in the Southern Hemisphere include the [[1998 United States embassy bombings]], which occurred simultaneously  in Kenya and Tanzania and killed 224, and the [[2002 Bali Bombings]] which killed 202.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://timesofmalta.com/article/us-intelligence-bali-attack-sophisticated.165114|title=US intelligence: Bali attack 'sophisticated'|date=October 15, 2002|website=Times of Malta}}</ref><ref>{{cite book

Certain areas of the Southern Hemisphere are vulnerable to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, and this is driven by intense tectonic activity along the southern [[Pacific Ring of Fire]]. One of the most notable seismic events is the [[1960 Valdivia earthquake]] in Chile, which remains the most powerful earthquake ever recorded at 9.6 on the [[moment magnitude scale]]. The event caused an estimated 1,000 to 6,000 deaths mainly in Chile, as well as tsunamis which had varying impacts across the Pacific Rim, including in Australia and areas above the equator like Hawaii, Japan, the Philippines and the Aleutian Islands.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ga.gov.au/news/how-the-worlds-largest-earthquake-made-waves-in-australia|title=How the world's largest earthquake made waves in Australia|first=Geoscience|last=Australia|date=May 22, 2020|website=Geoscience Australia}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/event/Chile-earthquake-of-1960|title=Chile earthquake of 1960 | Causes, Effects, & Facts | Britannica|website=www.britannica.com}}</ref> The [[1970 Ancash earthquake]] and [[1970 Huascarán debris avalanche|Huascarán debris avalanche]] in Peru resulted in up to 70,000 fatalities and is the deadliest natural disaster to have occurred entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-latin-america-52839770|title=In pictures: Peru's most catastrophic natural disaster|date=May 30, 2020|via=www.bbc.com}}</ref> In more recent times, the [[2009 Samoa earthquake and tsunami]] caused at least 189 fatalities, the [[2010 Chile Earthquake]] caused 525 fatalities and the [[2011 Christchurch earthquake]] in New Zealand caused 185 fatalities.<ref name="muertos">{{Cite web|url=http://www.interior.gob.cl/filesapp/listado_fallecidos_desaparecidos_27Feb.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121114043429/http://www.interior.gob.cl/filesapp/listado_fallecidos_desaparecidos_27Feb.pdf|url-status=dead|title=Subsecretaría del Interior de Chile (31 January 2011). ; [[Africa]] : About one-third of the continent, from south of [[Mogadishu]] in [[Somalia]] in the east to south of [[Libreville]] in [[Gabon]] in the west. From the [[Equator]] ([[Latitude]]: 0°) to [[Cape Agulhas]] ([[Latitude]]: 34°50′S).

: The entire continent and its associated islands are within the Southern Hemisphere. From [[Prime Head]], at the northern tip of the [[Trinity Peninsula]] ([[Latitude]]: 63°12′48″S) to the [[South Pole]] ([[Latitude]]: 90° S).
; [[Asia]]
: The entire continental mainland is within the [[Northern Hemisphere]]; only the southern portion of [[Maritime Southeast Asia]], including [[Timor-Leste]] and most of [[Indonesia]], plus the [[British Indian Ocean Territory]] and [[atolls of the Maldives|two out of 26 atolls]] of the Maldives, part of the [[Indian subcontinent]] in the [[Indian Ocean]], are in the Southern Hemisphere. : The entire continent and most of its associated islands are within the Southern Hemisphere. From the [[Equator]] ([[Latitude]]: 0°) to [[Bishop and Clerk Islets]], Tasmania, Australia ([[Latitude]]: 55°03′ S).

: Most of the continent, from south of the [[Amazon River]] mouth in [[Brazil]] in the east to north of [[Quito]] in Ecuador in the west. : The entire [[submerged continent]], including [[New Caledonia]], [[New Zealand]], [[Norfolk Island]], and other associated low-lying islands above sea level, is within the Southern Hemisphere.
